q.q: Which ART technique involves transferring a donor ovum into another female's fallopian tube for fertilisation to occur within her body?
q.e: In GIFT, a donor ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce her own ova but can support fertilisation/development.

q.q: ICSI is most appropriately used when:
o: The fallopian tubes are completely blocked
Sperm count/motility is too poor for natural fertilisation
q.e: ICSI (direct injection of sperm into the ovum's cytoplasm) is used when sperm are too few or weak to fertilise the ovum unassisted.

q.q: Consider the following statements about the aims of the RCH programme: (i) spreading knowledge about pre-natal and post-natal care and the importance of breast feeding; (ii) creating awareness about population explosion and its consequences; (iii) discouraging equal opportunity for the male and female child; (iv) providing medical assistance for infertility, especially in rural areas. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (ii) and (iv) are genuine RCH aims. Statement (iii) is reversed — RCH actually promotes, not discourages, equal opportunity for the male and female child.

q.q: A fall in the number of illegal abortions performed and a reduction in the incidence of infertility in a population are both regarded as:
o: Side effects of oral contraceptive pills
q.e: Reduced number of illegal abortions and reduced infertility are both listed among the indicators of improved reproductive health of a society.

q.q: The RCH programme emphasises that a reproductively healthy society needs ‘correct scientific knowledge about reproduction’ and not just healthy organs. Which specific aim of the programme reflects this emphasis?
o: Providing medical assistance for problems of pregnancy alone
Promoting equal opportunity for the male and female child
Creating awareness among people about reproductive organs, adolescence and reproductive processes
Imposing a statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination
q.e: Creating awareness among people about reproductive organs, adolescence and reproductive processes is the RCH aim that builds correct scientific knowledge, as distinct from purely medical or legal measures.

q.q: A rural health centre conducts special counselling sessions for new mothers on the importance of breast feeding and proper post-natal care. This directly addresses which RCH aim?
o: Imposing a statutory ban on amniocentesis
Spreading knowledge about pre-natal and post-natal care of the mother and child
q.e: One of the RCH aims is spreading knowledge about pre-natal and post-natal care of the mother and child, and the importance of breast feeding — exactly what this counselling session addresses.

q.q: Introducing sex education in schools, as an explicit aim of the RCH programme, is meant mainly to:
o: Give correct information and discourage myths and misconceptions about sex-related issues
Reduce the school-going age of children
Replace the need for family planning programmes
Directly increase the country's birth rate
q.e: Sex education in schools aims to give correct information to students and to discourage myths and misconceptions about sex-related issues.

q.q: Population explosion directly leads to scarcity of basic requirements such as food, shelter and clothing, and also increases:
o: Availability of natural resources per person
The number of fertility clinics automatically
q.e: Population explosion causes scarcity of basic requirements and increases unemployment, poverty and pressure on natural resources.

q.q: A government campaign uses posters, films and hoardings showing a happy small family, alongside the slogan ‘HUM DO HAMARE DO’. This strategy is part of:
o: Advertising for a new oral contraceptive brand only
A campaign to increase the marriageable age
Education and motivation campaigns to check population explosion
q.e: Advertisement through posters, films and hoardings promoting a small, happy family is part of the intensive education and motivation campaigns used to check population explosion.

q.q: A state government provides additional financial benefits specifically to couples who choose to have only one or two children. This measure is intended to:
o: Directly cure infertility in the couple
Replace the need for the RCH programme
Encourage smaller families and help check population explosion
q.e: Incentives to couples with smaller families are among the steps taken to overcome population explosion.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) Contraceptives are a routine requirement for every reproductively healthy person. (ii) Contraceptives are used to avoid pregnancy or to space children. (iii) A contraceptive method should ideally be chosen after consulting a qualified medical professional. (iv) All artificial contraceptive methods are completely free of any side effects. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (ii) and (iii) are correct. Statement (i) is false — contraceptives are not a routine requirement. Statement (iv) is false — possible ill effects like nausea, abdominal pain and breakthrough bleeding can occur.

q.q: According to the chapter, a contraceptive method should ideally be chosen only after:
o: Reading an advertisement in a newspaper
Checking its price at a local pharmacy
q.e: The chapter emphasises that the choice of a contraceptive method should always be made under consultation with a qualified medical professional.

q.q: ‘Nirodh’ is a popular Indian brand name for which contraceptive device?
q.e: ‘Nirodh’ is a popular brand of the male condom in India.

q.q: Despite the intention to withdraw the penis before ejaculation, coitus interruptus has a relatively high failure rate mainly because:
o: It requires a doctor to be present during coitus
It permanently damages the vas deferens
It always causes heavy breakthrough bleeding
Pre-ejaculatory fluid may already contain sperms, and the withdrawal may be mistimed
q.e: Coitus interruptus fails frequently because pre-ejaculatory fluid can contain sperms and because withdrawal timing is often inaccurate.

q.q: Amenorrhea, the basis of the term ‘lactational amenorrhea method’, refers to:
q.e: Amenorrhea means absence of menstruation; during intense lactation after parturition, the mother does not menstruate and does not ovulate.

q.q: A condom used by a female partner, unlike the male condom which covers the penis, is designed to cover:
q.e: Condoms are used to cover the penis in the male, or to cover the vagina and cervix in the female, just before coitus.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) Natural methods use no drug or device and hence have no side effects. (ii) Barrier methods are available for both males and females. (iii) Vaults are a type of hormone-releasing IUD. (iv) Spermicidal creams increase the contraceptive efficiency of diaphragms. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (ii) and (iv) are correct. Statement (iii) is false — vaults are barrier devices like diaphragms and cervical caps, not IUDs.

q.q: Copper-releasing IUDs such as CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375 prevent conception mainly because the released copper ions:
o: Directly kill the ovum before ovulation
Permanently block the cervix with scar tissue
Increase the secretion of gonadotropic hormones
Suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms
q.e: In copper-releasing IUDs like CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375, the released Cu ions suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.

q.q: LNG-20, a hormone-releasing IUD that releases levonorgestrel at 20 µg/day, is also sold under the trade name:
q.e: LNG-20 (Levonorgestrel 20 µg/day) is a hormone-releasing IUD also sold under the trade name Minera.

q.q: A newly married woman wants to delay her first pregnancy for a few years and later space her children well, without undergoing any permanent procedure. Which category of contraceptive is described as ideal for exactly this purpose?
q.e: IUDs are described as ideal contraceptives for females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children, without the permanence of surgical methods.

q.q: Unlike most oral contraceptive pills that must be taken daily for 21 days each cycle, Saheli is unique among hormonal contraceptives in this chapter because it is taken:
o: Only on the day of ovulation
q.e: Saheli, developed at CDRI Lucknow, is a ‘once a week’ non-steroidal pill, unlike the daily-for-21-days regimen of standard oral contraceptive pills.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) Non-medicated IUDs like the Lippes loop are spermicidal through a sterile inflammatory response. (ii) Hormone-releasing IUDs make the cervix hostile to sperms. (iii) Injectable and implant contraceptives must be administered daily. (iv) Emergency contraception can involve inserting an IUD within 72 hours of coitus. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (ii) and (iv) are correct. Statement (iii) is false — injectables/implants act for months to years per dose, not daily.

q.q: India legalised Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) in 1971, attaching strict conditions to it mainly in order to:
o: Check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticide
Encourage more couples to undergo surgical sterilisation
Make amniocentesis freely available for sex determination
Increase the country's overall birth rate
q.e: MTP was legalised in India in 1971 with strict conditions attached, mainly to check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticide.

q.q: MTP is considered a ‘healthy trend’ when it helps a woman get rid of an unwanted pregnancy arising from:
o: Casual unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, or rape
Successful use of the rhythm method
q.e: A healthy trend of MTP is helping get rid of unwanted pregnancies arising from casual unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, or rape.

q.q: MTP is considered essential, rather than merely elective, in situations where:
o: The couple simply wants to choose the baby's sex
The pregnancy has crossed the second trimester
Continuation of the pregnancy could be harmful or even fatal to the mother, the foetus, or both
The mother wishes to avoid a caesarean delivery
q.e: MTP is essential in situations where continuation of the pregnancy could be harmful or even fatal either to the mother, the foetus, or both.

q.q: Which combination of measures is suggested in the chapter to help reverse the unhealthy trends associated with MTP, such as illegal abortions by quacks?
o: Banning all forms of MTP completely
Removing the MTP Act's legal conditions entirely
Making amniocentesis compulsory for every pregnancy
Effective counselling, stricter enforcement, and more healthcare facilities
q.e: Effective counselling about avoiding unprotected coitus and the risks of illegal abortion, together with stricter enforcement and more healthcare facilities, could help reverse the unhealthy trends of MTP.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) Vasectomy and tubectomy are generally reversible procedures. (ii) Surgical sterilisation is chosen mainly by couples who have completed their family. (iii) Around 45–50 million MTPs are performed worldwide every year. (iv) Illegal MTPs by unqualified quacks are considered a healthy trend. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (ii) and (iii) are correct. Statement (i) is false — sterilisation is generally irreversible. Statement (iv) is false — illegal MTPs by quacks are an unhealthy trend.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the examples of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) in this chapter?
q.e: Examples of STDs include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV. Malaria is a mosquito-borne disease, not an STD.

q.q: Itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swelling in the genital region are described in this chapter as:
o: Symptoms unrelated to any reproductive tract infection
Signs of a successful oral contraceptive regimen
q.e: Early symptoms of STDs are often minor: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swelling in the genital region.

q.q: If a person notices early symptoms that might indicate an STD, the chapter recommends that they should:
o: Wait at least two years before seeking any advice
Undergo amniocentesis to confirm the diagnosis
Consult a qualified doctor immediately for detection and complete treatment
q.e: Prevention and management of STDs includes consulting a qualified doctor immediately for early detection and complete treatment if symptoms are suspected.

q.q: An intravenous drug user regularly shares needles and syringes with other users. Besides unsafe sexual contact, this practice places the person at heightened risk of which two infections mentioned in this chapter?
q.e: Hepatitis-B and HIV can additionally spread through sharing infected needles/syringes, unlike the other STDs listed.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) STDs are also known as reproductive tract infections (RTIs). (ii) Symptoms of STDs are always severe and obvious in females. (iii) STDs can spread from an infected mother to her foetus. (iv) Avoiding sex with unknown or multiple partners helps prevent STDs. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (iii) and (iv) are correct. Statement (ii) is false — symptoms are often absent or mild in females, which is why detection is frequently delayed.

q.q: Consider the following statements about causes of infertility: (i) Non-functional testes can be a cause in men. (ii) Injuries or disease of the ovaries can be a cause in women. (iii) A physical abnormality of the penis can be a cause in men. (iv) Blockage of the fallopian tube can be a cause in men. How many of the above statements are correctly matched?
q.e: Statements (i), (ii) and (iii) are correctly matched. Statement (iv) is wrong — a blocked fallopian tube is a cause of infertility in women, not men.

q.q: Injuries or disease of the ovaries, and non-ovulatory menstrual cycles, are listed in this chapter as causes of infertility specific to:
q.e: Endocrine disorders, injuries or disease of the ovaries, and non-ovulatory menstrual cycles are listed among the causes of infertility in women.

q.q: A couple has been trying to conceive for over two years through regular, unprotected intercourse, without success. According to this chapter, their most appropriate next step would be to:
o: Approach a fertility clinic for diagnosis and possible ART treatment
Assume pregnancy is impossible and take no further action
q.e: Couples affected by infertility can approach specialised fertility clinics, which diagnose and treat the underlying cause, and Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART) can help them have children.

q.q: A man's endocrine system shows hyposecretion of gonadotropic hormones. Based on this chapter, this hormonal disorder is listed as a cause of infertility affecting:
q.e: Endocrine disorders such as hyposecretion of gonadotropic hormones are listed among the causes of infertility in men.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) Oligospermia and asthenozoospermia both refer to abnormalities of sperm, but not to their complete absence. (ii) A tumour in the uterus can be a cause of infertility in women. (iii) Impotency means the inability to attain or hold an erection long enough for intercourse. (iv) All causes of infertility listed in this chapter are permanent and untreatable. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct. Statement (iv) is false — fertility clinics and ART can treat many causes of infertility.

q.q: The acronym GIFT, an ART technique described in this chapter, stands for:
q.e: GIFT stands for Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer, in which a donor ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube of a recipient female.

q.q: The acronym ZIFT, an ART technique described in this chapter, stands for:
q.e: ZIFT stands for Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer, in which a laboratory-formed zygote (up to the 8-blastomere stage) is transferred into the fallopian tube.

q.q: The term ‘in vitro’ in In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) literally indicates that fertilisation of the ovum by the sperm takes place:
o: Inside the fallopian tube of the female
Outside the body, under laboratory conditions
Inside the testes of the male
q.e: In Vitro Fertilisation means fertilisation occurring outside the body, in a laboratory, followed by transfer of the embryo into the reproductive tract.

q.q: Consider the following statements: (i) IVF is popularly known as the test tube baby method. (ii) ZIFT transfers the zygote into the uterus, not the fallopian tube. (iii) GIFT is useful for a female who cannot produce her own ova. (iv) ICSI involves direct injection of a sperm into the cytoplasm of the ovum. How many of the above statements are correct?
q.e: Statements (i), (iii) and (iv) are correct. Statement (ii) is false — ZIFT transfers the zygote into the fallopian tube; IUT (not ZIFT) transfers embryos with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus.

q.q: Artificial Insemination (AI) differs conceptually from laboratory-based ART techniques such as IVF, ZIFT and GIFT mainly because in AI:
o: Fertilisation always occurs in a laboratory dish before transfer
A donor ovum must always be used
The embryo is always frozen before being used
Fertilisation occurs naturally inside the female's body after semen is introduced, without any laboratory handling of gametes
q.e: In AI, semen is simply introduced into the vagina or uterus and fertilisation then occurs naturally inside the body, unlike IVF/ZIFT/GIFT where gametes or embryos are handled in the laboratory.

q.q: Who is known as the 'Father of Genetics'?
q.e: Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years and is regarded as the father of genetics.

q.q: Genetics is the branch of biology that deals with:
o: Inheritance and variation of characters from parents to offspring
Evolution of species over geological time
q.e: Genetics is defined as the study of inheritance (passing of characters from parent to progeny) and variation (the degree to which progeny differ from parents).

q.q: Mendel carried out his hybridisation experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) over a period of:
q.e: Mendel's classical experiments on the garden pea were conducted over seven years, from 1856 to 1863.

q.q: An allele is best defined as:
o: The physical location of a gene on a chromosome
A functional unit of inheritance in general
Alternative forms of a gene at the same locus governing a contrasting trait
The overall genetic constitution of an organism
q.e: Alleles are slightly different forms of the same gene located at a specific locus on homologous chromosomes, determining alternate expression of a character, e.g., round and wrinkled seed shape.

q.q: Which of the following correctly explains why Mendel's conclusions were more reliable than earlier plant breeding studies?
o: He worked only with data from wild populations
He used statistical analysis and mathematical logic along with a large sample size
He studied only qualitative, non-heritable traits
He deliberately avoided using self-pollinating lines
q.e: Mendel was the first to apply statistical analysis and mathematical logic to biology, and his large sampling size gave credibility to his results.

q.q: Mendel selected garden pea for his experiments for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
o: It has several easily distinguishable contrasting characters
It is naturally self-pollinating but also allows artificial cross-pollination
It has a long life span, requiring many years to complete one generation
It produces a large number of seeds
q.e: Pea plants have a short life span, not a long one; this, along with easy cultivation, minimum space requirement, and many contrasting characters, made them ideal for Mendel's work.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Allele = alternative forms of a gene (3); Locus = specific region on a chromosome (1); Homozygous = paired genes similar, e.g. TT/tt (2); Heterozygous = paired genes dissimilar, e.g. Tt (4).

q.q: In Mendel's classical experiments on garden pea, which of the following dominant-recessive character pairs is correctly matched?
q.e: Round seed shape is dominant over wrinkled. The other options are reversed: pod colour is actually Green (dominant) to Yellow (recessive), flower position is Axial (dominant) to Terminal (recessive), and stem height is Tall (dominant) to Dwarf (recessive).

q.q: In a monohybrid cross between a true-breeding tall pea plant (TT) and a true-breeding dwarf pea plant (tt), the F1 generation is:
q.e: TT x tt crosses produce an F1 that is entirely Tt, and since tall is dominant, all F1 plants are tall.

q.q: Mendel's Law of Dominance states that:
o: Two alleles of a pair always segregate equally into gametes
Genes for different traits assort independently of each other
In a pair of dissimilar factors, one member dominates the other so only one parental character is expressed in F1
Alleles blend to give an intermediate phenotype in F1
q.e: The Law of Dominance explains why only one parental character (the dominant one) is expressed in F1, while both characters reappear in F2.

q.q: The Law of Segregation is also known as the Law of Purity of Gametes because:
o: Gametes always carry the dominant allele only
The two alleles of a gene pair separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele
Gametes from a heterozygous parent are genetically identical
Alleles from different genes always segregate together
q.e: During gamete formation, the two alleles of a pair segregate so that a gamete receives only one of the two factors; heterozygous parents produce two types of gametes in equal proportion.

q.q: In a test cross, an unknown tall pea plant is crossed with a dwarf (tt) plant. If all the progeny obtained are tall, the unknown parent's genotype is:
o: Cannot be determined from this cross
q.e: When TT (unknown) x tt is performed, all progeny are Tt (tall), showing the unknown parent is homozygous dominant; if it were heterozygous, a 1:1 tall:dwarf ratio would appear instead.

q.q: Guinea pig coat colour: BB (black) x bb (white) produces an F1 that is entirely black (Bb). On selfing the F1, which statement about the F2 generation is correct?
o: F2 shows a phenotypic ratio of 1 Black : 1 White only
F2 shows Black:White = 3:1 phenotypically and BB:Bb:bb = 1:2:1 genotypically
F2 shows all black progeny with no segregation at all
F2 shows an intermediate blackish-white coat colour
q.e: Coat colour in guinea pigs follows a standard monohybrid pattern: black is dominant over white, so selfing the heterozygous F1 gives the classic 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic F2 ratios.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Back cross is a cross between F1 and either parent (2); Test cross is a cross between a hybrid and a homozygous recessive parent, used to determine genotype (3); Out cross is a cross between a hybrid and a homozygous dominant parent (1).

q.q: In a monohybrid cross Tt x Tt, what fraction of the F2 offspring is expected to be homozygous recessive (tt)?
q.e: The F2 genotypic ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 1/4 of the offspring are homozygous recessive (tt), corresponding to the dwarf class in the 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

q.q: A dihybrid cross RRYY (round, yellow) x rryy (wrinkled, green) produces an F1 that is:
o: All RrYy, round, yellow, heterozygous for both traits
q.e: Crossing two true-breeding parents differing in two traits gives an F1 that is heterozygous for both genes and shows both dominant traits, round and yellow.

q.q: The classical F2 phenotypic ratio obtained in Mendel's dihybrid cross of pea (seed shape x seed colour) is:
q.e: Selfing the RrYy F1 gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9 Round-Yellow : 3 Round-Green : 3 Wrinkled-Yellow : 1 Wrinkled-Green.

q.q: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment states that:
o: Alleles of a gene pair always separate together during gamete formation
When two pairs of traits combine in a hybrid, one pair of traits segregates independently of the other pair
Dominant traits are always expressed over recessive ones
A heterozygous individual produces only one type of gamete
q.e: This law, based on the dihybrid cross, states that genes for one trait assort independently of genes for another trait during gamete formation.

q.q: A dihybrid RrYy pea plant, during gamete formation, produces gametes in which pattern?
o: Two gamete types, RY and ry, in equal proportion
Four gamete types, RY, Ry, rY and ry, in equal (25% each) proportion
Four gamete types in the ratio 9:3:3:1
q.e: Because the two gene pairs assort independently, a RrYy individual produces four gamete types, RY, Ry, rY and ry, each at 25% frequency.

q.q: Mendel's work, published in 1865 in the Proceedings of the Natural History Society of Brunn, remained unrecognised until 1900 mainly because:
o: He never performed enough replicated experiments
His idea of discrete, particulate factors clashed with the prevailing view of continuous variation, and his mathematical approach was not readily accepted
He refused to share his data with other scientists
The garden pea was considered an unsuitable experimental organism
q.e: Lack of communication and publicity, resistance to his discrete-factor concept, and reluctance to accept his mathematical approach kept Mendel's work obscure until Hugo de Vries, Correns, and Von Tschermak independently rediscovered it in 1900.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: RRYY is the pure dominant parental combination (3); rryy is the pure recessive parental combination (2); RrYy is heterozygous for both genes (1); RRyy is a new recombinant combination arising from independent assortment (4).

q.q: Out of the 16 F2 combinations obtained on selfing RrYy x RrYy, how many show the Wrinkled, Yellow phenotype?
q.e: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9 Round-Yellow : 3 Round-Green : 3 Wrinkled-Yellow : 1 Wrinkled-Green out of 16 total combinations, so 3 combinations are Wrinkled Yellow.

q.q: Incomplete dominance, in which the F1 phenotype is an intermediate blend of both parents, was discovered by Carl Correns in 1903 while working on:
q.e: Carl Correns discovered incomplete dominance in 1903 in Mirabilis jalapa, where RR (red) x rr (white) gives an all-pink F1.

q.q: Co-dominance is best described as a condition in which:
o: The heterozygote shows a completely new, blended phenotype
One allele completely masks the other in the heterozygote
Both alleles of a gene pair express themselves independently and fully in the heterozygote
Three or more alleles govern the same trait
q.e: In co-dominance, both alleles are equally conspicuous and express independently without mixing, as seen with I^A and I^B in the AB blood group.

q.q: Pleiotropy refers to a condition where:
o: A single gene influences more than one phenotypic trait
A single trait is controlled by more than two genes
Two genes are located very close together on a chromosome
A gene shows no dominant-recessive relationship with its allele
q.e: A pleiotropic gene affects metabolic pathways that influence multiple traits, as seen with the gene responsible for phenylketonuria (PKU), which affects both mental development and pigmentation.

q.q: In Mirabilis jalapa, RR (red) x rr (white) gives an all-pink F1 (Rr). On selfing the F1, which of the following is true of the F2 generation?
o: F2 phenotypic ratio is 3 Red : 1 White, same as a typical dominant cross
F2 phenotypic ratio, 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White, is exactly the same as the genotypic ratio, 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr
F2 shows only pink flowers with no segregation
q.e: Since dominance is incomplete, the phenotypic and genotypic ratios coincide (1:2:1), unlike complete dominance where the two ratios differ.

q.q: A person with genotype Hb^A Hb^S suffers only mild anaemia because some red blood cells sickle under low oxygen tension while the rest remain normal. This observation best illustrates that Hb^A and Hb^S are:
o: Showing incomplete dominance, producing an intermediate haemoglobin
Co-dominant, since both haemoglobin types are produced and expressed independently
Linked genes located on the same chromosome
Multiple alleles with no functional difference
q.e: In the heterozygote, both Hb^A and Hb^S haemoglobin types are produced and detectable, proving the two alleles are co-dominant rather than blending into a new intermediate form.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Incomplete dominance is seen in Mirabilis flower colour (3); co-dominance in the AB blood group (1); pleiotropy in PKU, a single gene affecting multiple traits (4); polygenic inheritance in human skin colour (2).

q.q: In the ABO blood group system, an individual with genotype I^A I^B will show which blood group phenotype?
q.e: I^A and I^B are co-dominant, so an individual with genotype I^A I^B expresses both A and B antigens, giving blood group AB.

q.q: The chromosomal theory of inheritance, proposing that genes and chromosomes both occur in pairs and segregate in a parallel manner, was put forward by:
q.e: Sutton and Boveri observed that chromosome behaviour parallels gene behaviour and proposed that the pairing and separation of chromosomes leads to segregation of the gene pairs they carry.

q.q: Thomas Hunt Morgan is regarded as the 'father of experimental genetics' for his work on:
q.e: Morgan's dihybrid cross experiments on Drosophila melanogaster established the physical basis of linkage and sex-linked inheritance.

q.q: Linkage refers to:
o: The generation of new, non-parental gene combinations
The physical association of genes located on the same chromosome
The independent segregation of two gene pairs
The blending of two alleles in a heterozygote
q.e: Linkage is the physical association of genes on a chromosome, which causes them to be inherited together more often than expected by independent assortment.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT a reason Morgan chose Drosophila melanogaster for his genetic studies?
o: It can be grown on simple synthetic medium in the laboratory
Its life cycle is completed in about two weeks
It shows very few hereditary variations, making analysis simpler
A single mating produces a large number of progeny
q.e: Drosophila was chosen because its hereditary variations are clearly visible under a low power microscope, along with easy lab culturing, a short two-week life cycle, and high progeny numbers, not because it shows few variations.

q.q: In Morgan's dihybrid cross of Drosophila, genes for body colour (y) and eye colour (w) showed 98.7% parental type and 1.3% recombinant type, while eye colour (w) and wing size (m) showed 62.8% parental and 37.2% recombinant type. This indicates that:
o: y and w are loosely linked while w and m are tightly linked
y and w are more tightly linked than w and m
y, w and m all assort completely independently of each other
Recombination frequency has no relation to gene distance
q.e: A lower recombination frequency (1.3%) between y and w indicates they are tightly linked, whereas the higher recombination frequency (37.2%) between w and m indicates looser linkage.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Sutton and Boveri proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance (2); Morgan demonstrated sex-linked inheritance in Drosophila (3); Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map gene positions on chromosomes (1).

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: 1% crossing over equals 1 map unit, or 1 centi Morgan (3); 10% crossing over equals 1 deci Morgan (1); 100% crossing over equals 1 Morgan (2).

q.q: In Morgan's Drosophila cross data, genes y and w showed 1.3% recombinants while genes w and m showed 37.2% recombinants. Based on Sturtevant's mapping principle, which conclusion is correct?
o: Genes y and w are physically farther apart than w and m
Genes w and m are physically farther apart than y and w
Recombination frequency is unrelated to physical distance between genes
Both gene pairs are equidistant on the chromosome
q.e: Since the frequency of crossing over increases with the physical distance between two genes, the higher recombination frequency (37.2%) between w and m shows they are farther apart than y and w (1.3%).

q.q: In humans, sex determination follows the:
q.e: Human females are XX and males are XY; all ova carry X, while sperm are 50% X-bearing and 50% Y-bearing.

q.q: The genetic/chromosomal basis of sex determination was first discovered by Henking, who observed a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis in insects and named it the:
q.e: Henking observed that only 50% of sperm obtained this structure after spermatogenesis; it was later found to be a chromosome and named the X chromosome.

q.q: In the ZW type of sex determination seen in birds, which sex is heterogametic?
q.e: In the ZW type, the female has one Z and one W chromosome (heterogametic), while the male has a pair of Z chromosomes (homogametic).

q.q: In the haplodiploid sex-determination system of honey bees, which statement is correct?
o: Both males and females develop from fertilised eggs and are diploid
Females develop from fertilised eggs, diploid with 32 chromosomes, while males develop from unfertilised eggs by parthenogenesis, haploid with 16 chromosomes
Males are diploid and females are haploid
Sex is determined by a pair of allosomes, as in humans
q.e: In honey bees, sex is determined by the number of chromosome sets received: fertilised eggs develop into diploid females (32 chromosomes) while unfertilised eggs develop into haploid males (16 chromosomes) through parthenogenesis.

q.q: A male honey bee (drone) produces sperm by mitosis and develops from an unfertilised egg. Which of the following statements about the drone is correct?
o: A drone has a father but cannot have sons or grandsons
A drone has no father, cannot have sons, but can have grandsons
A drone has both a father and can have sons
A drone is always diploid like the queen
q.e: Since drones develop from unfertilised eggs, they have no father and hence cannot produce sons, but they can have grandsons through their daughters.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: XO type is seen in Grasshopper and Earthworm (1); XY type in Humans and Drosophila (2); ZW type in Birds (3); Haplodiploid type in Honey bee (4).

q.q: In a human cross between an XY father and an XX mother, what is the expected phenotypic ratio of sons to daughters?
q.e: All ova carry X, while 50% of sperm carry X and 50% carry Y, giving an expected 1:1 ratio of XX (daughters) to XY (sons).

q.q: Mutation is defined as:
o: The random shuffling of chromosomes during meiosis
An alteration in the DNA sequence resulting in a change in genotype and phenotype
The transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
q.e: Mutation is an alteration of the DNA sequence that results in changes in the genotype and, consequently, the phenotype of an organism.

q.q: A point mutation, such as the one causing sickle cell anaemia, results from:
o: Deletion of a large chromosome segment
A change in a single base pair of DNA
q.e: Point mutations arise from a change in a single base pair of DNA; the sickle cell anaemia mutation is a classic example.

q.q: A frameshift mutation is caused by:
o: A change in a single base pair without altering the reading frame
Deletion or insertion of a base pair in the DNA sequence
q.e: Frameshift mutations result from the deletion or insertion of a base pair in the DNA sequence, which shifts the reading frame of the gene.

q.q: Nitrous acid is classified as a mutagen because it:
o: Is a physical mutagen that causes ionizing damage to DNA
Is a chemical, deaminating agent that converts cytosine to uracil in DNA
Is a biological mutagen similar to a virus
Has no effect on the DNA sequence
q.e: Nitrous acid is a chemical mutagen and a deaminating agent that converts cytosine to uracil, altering the DNA sequence.

q.q: In a pedigree chart, two offspring symbols are shown joined at a single point, which itself joins upward to a single vertical line leading to the parents. This pattern most likely represents:
q.e: When two offspring symbols are joined at a point that itself connects upward to a single line, it denotes monozygotic (identical) twins, as opposed to dizygotic twins which are joined at separate points on the horizontal line.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Square represents Male (3); Circle represents Female (1); Diamond represents sex unspecified (4); a filled/shaded shape represents an Affected individual (2).

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Physical mutagens include UV radiation and gamma rays (2); chemical mutagens include nitrous acid (1); biological mutagens include viruses like HPV and bacteria like Helicobacter (3).

q.q: In a pedigree chart, an individual is represented by a diamond symbol with the number '3' written inside it. This notation indicates:
o: Three affected individuals of unspecified sex
Three unaffected offspring of unspecified sex
Three generations have been studied in this pedigree
q.e: A number written inside a diamond in a pedigree chart represents that many unaffected offspring of unspecified sex.

q.q: Down's syndrome is caused by:
o: Trisomy of chromosome 21, an extra copy
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
q.e: Down's syndrome, first described by Langdon Down in 1866, results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, an autosomal trisomy.

q.q: Klinefelter's syndrome is characterised by the karyotype:
q.e: Klinefelter's syndrome results from an additional X chromosome, giving 47 chromosomes (XXY), an allosomal trisomy.

q.q: Turner's syndrome results from:
o: Absence of one X chromosome, 45 chromosomes (XO)
q.e: Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome, giving 45 chromosomes (XO), an allosomal monosomy.

q.q: Haemophilia A, also called the 'Royal disease', is caused by a deficiency of which clotting protein, and follows which inheritance pattern?
q.e: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder in which the blood clotting protein Factor VIII is affected, so even a simple cut can cause uncontrolled bleeding.

q.q: A phenotypically normal woman, whose father was colour blind, marries a man with normal vision. What is the chance that their son will be colour blind?
q.e: Since her father was colour blind, the woman is an obligate carrier (heterozygous); a son has a 50% chance of inheriting the recessive X-linked allele and being colour blind.

q.q: A pedigree shows a trait appearing in every generation, transmitted by affected individuals of either sex, with roughly equal numbers of affected males and females. This pattern is most consistent with:
q.e: Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation, a vertical pedigree pattern, and affect males and females equally, since transmission does not depend on the sex of the parent or offspring.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Down's syndrome results from trisomy of chromosome 21 (2); Turner's syndrome from monosomy of the X chromosome, 45 XO (3); Klinefelter's syndrome from trisomy of sex chromosomes, 47 XXY (4); Cri du chat syndrome from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (1).

q.q: A karyotype analysis of an individual shows 45 chromosomes, with a single X chromosome and no Y chromosome. This karyotype is consistent with:
q.e: A 45, XO karyotype, absence of one X chromosome, is the defining feature of Turner's syndrome, an allosomal monosomy.

q.q: According to Mendel's seven contrasting characters in garden pea, which trait is dominant for flower colour?
q.e: In Mendel's classical pea experiments, violet flower colour is dominant over white.

q.q: According to Mendel's seven contrasting characters in garden pea, which trait is dominant for pod shape?
q.e: For pod shape, the inflated (full) pod is dominant over the constricted pod, as recorded in Mendel's seven contrasting character pairs.

q.q: In genetics, the degree by which the progeny differs from its parents is termed:
q.e: Variation is defined as the degree by which the progeny differs from its parents, as distinguished from inheritance (the process by which characters are passed from parent to progeny).

q.q: Which of the following correctly defines a 'hybrid' in genetics, as used in Mendel's experiments?
o: The genetic constitution of an organism, expressed using symbols
The offspring of two parents differing in one or more characters, e.g. TT x tt giving Tt
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene, e.g. TT
A gene which fails to express itself in the presence of a dominant gene
q.e: A hybrid is the offspring of two parents differing in one or more characters -- for example, crossing TT x tt produces a hybrid with genotype Tt.

q.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'dominant gene' from a 'dominant character'?
o: A dominant gene is homozygous only, while a dominant character can be heterozygous only
A dominant gene expresses itself in the presence of a contrasting (recessive) gene, while a dominant character is completely expressed even in the presence of a recessive allele
A dominant gene is found only in F2, while a dominant character is found only in F1
There is no difference; the two terms are used interchangeably in all contexts
q.e: A dominant gene is one that expresses itself in the presence of a contrasting gene, whereas a dominant character is a character that is completely expressed even in the presence of a recessive allele -- related but distinct concepts.

q.q: Which Indian cattle breed, developed in Punjab through artificial selection of naturally occurring variations -- long before genetics was formally understood -- is cited as an early example of humans exploiting heredity?
q.e: Humans knew as early as 8000-1000 B.C. that variation was linked to sexual reproduction, and exploited it to selectively breed plants and animals; the Sahiwal cow of Punjab is cited as an example of such artificial selection giving rise to an Indian breed.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Gene = functional unit of inheritance (3); Phenotype = external, observable appearance, expressed in words (4); Genotype = genetic constitution, expressed by symbols (1); Hybrid = offspring of two parents differing in one or more characters (2).

q.q: A garden pea plant bears flowers positioned along the side of the stem (at the axil of the leaf), rather than only at the tip. According to Mendel's classical results, this flower position (axial) is the:
o: A trait not studied by Mendel
q.e: Of Mendel's seven contrasting character pairs, axial flower position is dominant over terminal flower position.

q.q: A pea plant produces green seeds and has yellow pods. Based on Mendel's classical dominant-recessive character pairs, which statement about these two traits is correct?
o: Seed colour (green) is recessive, and pod colour (yellow) is dominant
Both traits shown are recessive traits
Both traits shown are dominant traits
Seed colour (green) is dominant, and pod colour (yellow) is recessive
q.e: Yellow seed colour is dominant over green, and green pod colour is dominant over yellow. So a plant with green seeds and yellow pods is showing the recessive form of BOTH characters.

q.q: According to Mendel's seven contrasting characters in garden pea, which trait is dominant for seed colour?
q.e: For seed colour, yellow is dominant over green, as recorded in Mendel's seven contrasting character pairs.

q.q: The Punnett square method for calculating the probability of genotype combinations in a cross is also known, in the source material, by which alternative name?
q.e: The Punnett square, developed by British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett, is also referred to as the Checker board method.

q.q: Statement I: Mendel's Law of Dominance and Law of Segregation are both based on the monohybrid cross. Statement II: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment is based on the dihybrid cross. Which is correct?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
q.e: The Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation are both derived from the monohybrid cross, while the Law of Independent Assortment is derived from the dihybrid cross.

q.q: In a monohybrid cross Tt x Tt, what fraction of the F2 offspring is expected to be heterozygous (Tt)?
q.e: The F2 genotypic ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 1/2 (2 out of 4) of the offspring are expected to be heterozygous (Tt).

q.q: In guinea pigs, a heterozygous black-coated individual (Bb) is test-crossed with a homozygous white-coated individual (bb). What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
q.e: As in any test cross of a heterozygote (Bb) with the homozygous recessive (bb), half the gametes carry B and half carry b, giving a 1 Black (Bb) : 1 White (bb) ratio -- confirming the unknown parent was heterozygous.

q.q: In the parental cross of homozygous black (BB) and homozygous white (bb) guinea pigs, which statement correctly describes the gametes produced?
o: Each sperm carries B, and each egg carries B
Each sperm carries b, and each egg carries b
Each sperm carries B, and each egg carries b (or vice versa, depending on parental sex)
Sperm and eggs both carry a mixture of B and b in equal numbers
q.e: In the cross between homozygous black (BB) and homozygous white (bb) guinea pigs, all gametes from the BB parent carry B, and all gametes from the bb parent carry b, giving an F1 that is entirely heterozygous (Bb).

q.q: In the cross TT (tall) x tt (dwarf), what type of gamete is produced by the tt parent?
o: Both T and t in equal proportion
q.e: A homozygous parent produces only one type of gamete; the tt parent, being homozygous recessive, produces gametes carrying only the t allele.

q.q: In a monohybrid cross Tt x Tt, what fraction of the F2 offspring is expected to show the dominant phenotype (tall)?
q.e: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 3 Tall : 1 Dwarf, so 3/4 of the offspring are expected to show the dominant (tall) phenotype.

q.q: Mendel's Law of Dominance explains why the F1 generation of a monohybrid cross shows only one parental character, while the F2 generation shows:
o: Both parental characters, in a 3:1 ratio
Neither parental character, but a new blended character
q.e: The Law of Dominance explains the expression of only one parental character in F1 (e.g. all tall), and the expression of both parental characters in F2 (tall and dwarf, in a 3:1 ratio).

q.q: In the binomial expression (ax + by)^2, used to derive the F2 genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross, 'a' and 'b' represent the gamete-bearing genes T and t, each at a frequency of:
q.e: In (ax + by)^2, 'a' and 'b' are the gamete-bearing genes T or t, each occurring at a frequency of 1/2 (since a heterozygous parent produces two types of gametes in equal proportion).

q.q: In the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy, what fraction of the offspring is expected to be heterozygous for BOTH genes (RrYy)?
q.e: In the full F2 genotypic ratio (1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 out of 16), the doubly heterozygous class RrYy occurs with a frequency of 4 out of 16, i.e. 1/4.

q.q: Out of the 16 F2 combinations obtained on selfing RrYy x RrYy, how many show the Round, Green phenotype?
q.e: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9 Round-Yellow : 3 Round-Green : 3 Wrinkled-Yellow : 1 Wrinkled-Green out of 16 total combinations, so 3 combinations are Round Green.

q.q: In 1900, Mendel's work was independently rediscovered by which three scientists?
o: Charles Darwin, Alfred Wallace and Francis Galton
Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak
Thomas Morgan, Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri
Karl Landsteiner, Felix Bernstein and Alfred Sturtevant
q.e: In 1900, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, working independently, rediscovered Mendel's laws of inheritance.

q.q: Which of the following correctly describes Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, based on the dihybrid cross for seed shape and seed colour?
o: Genes for shape and colour always segregate together, since they are on the same chromosome
Genes for shape do not intermix with genes for colour, but assort independently of each other during gamete formation
The dominant allele for shape always segregates with the dominant allele for colour
Genes for shape and colour show a 3:1 ratio identical to a monohybrid cross
q.e: The Law of Independent Assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, genes for one trait (e.g. shape) do not intermix with genes for another trait (e.g. colour), but assort independently of each other, each segregating in its own 3:1 pattern.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Round Yellow occupies 9 of the 16 F2 combinations (3); Round Green occupies 3 combinations (1); Wrinkled Green occupies 1 combination (4); Wrinkled Yellow occupies 3 combinations (2).

q.q: Out of the 16 F2 combinations obtained on selfing RrYy x RrYy, how many show the Wrinkled, Green phenotype (the pure recessive, parental type)?
q.e: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1, so only 1 out of the 16 combinations shows the Wrinkled, Green phenotype -- the pure recessive type, matching one of the original parents (rryy).

q.q: In a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy, the Punnett square of 16 F2 combinations represents how many distinct F2 genotypes?
q.e: Although there are 16 boxes in the Punnett square, the full F2 genotypic ratio (1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1) has 9 distinct terms, i.e. 9 distinct genotypes.

q.q: In Mendel's classical dihybrid cross experiment, the Parent (P) generation consisted of which two genotypes?
q.e: Mendel's dihybrid cross began with a homozygous round, yellow-seeded plant (RRYY) crossed with a homozygous wrinkled, green-seeded plant (rryy) as the Parent (P) generation.

q.q: According to the molecular explanation of dominance in the source material, a recessive phenotype is typically seen because the modified (recessive) allele:
o: Always produces a completely different, novel protein with a new function
Produces either a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all, so the phenotype depends on the unmodified (dominant) allele's functioning
Physically blends with the dominant allele's protein product
Is located on a different chromosome from the dominant allele
q.e: When a gene's modified allele produces a non-functional enzyme, or no enzyme at all, the recessive phenotype results because the observable trait depends only on the functioning of the unmodified, dominant allele.

q.q: A modified allele that produces a normal or only slightly less efficient enzyme -- resulting in the SAME phenotype as the original allele -- is referred to, in the source material, as an:
q.e: When the enzyme produced by a modified allele functions the same way as that produced by the original allele, the modified allele is called an 'equivalent allele', since it produces the same phenotype.

q.q: Multiple allelism (gene polymorphism), the expression of a single gene in more than two alternative forms, is typically detected only when:
o: A single individual is studied in isolation
The gene is located on a sex chromosome
q.e: Multiple allelism is found only when population studies are made, since more than two alleles of a gene can exist in a population even though any one individual carries only two of them.

q.q: The ABO blood group system, controlled by the gene 'I' with three alleles (I^A, I^B, i), gives rise to how many genotypes and how many phenotypes respectively?
q.e: There are 6 possible genotypes (I^A I^A, I^A i, I^B I^B, I^B i, I^A I^B, ii) for the ABO gene, but only 4 phenotypes (A, B, AB, O), since I^A and i together, and I^B and i together, each produce the same phenotype (A and B respectively).

q.q: Which of the following statements about ABO blood group inheritance is INCORRECT?
o: Heterozygous 'A' (I^A i) parents can produce both 'A' and 'O' progeny
'AB' (I^A I^B) parents can produce 'A', 'B' and 'AB' progeny, but never 'O'
Homozygous 'O' (ii) parents can only produce 'O' progeny
Homozygous 'A' (I^A I^A) parents can produce 'A', 'B' or 'O' progeny
q.e: Homozygous 'A' (I^A I^A) parents can only pass on the I^A allele, so they produce only 'A' progeny -- never 'B' or 'O'. The other three statements correctly describe ABO inheritance patterns.

q.q: Statement I: The ABO blood group system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901. Statement II: The precise inheritance pattern of the ABO blood group was worked out by Felix Bernstein in 1924. Which is correct?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
q.e: Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901, and Felix Bernstein worked out its precise inheritance pattern in 1924 -- both statements are correct.

q.q: F. Galton, who studied polygenic inheritance in man, coined which term for the application of genetics to attempt to improve the hereditary qualities of humans?
q.e: F. Galton studied polygenic inheritance in humans and coined the term 'eugenics' for the application of genetics to attempt to improve the hereditary qualities of humans.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Incomplete dominance produces a fine mixture of the two alleles' expression (2); Co-dominance shows no mixing of the effect of the two alleles (4); Incomplete dominance results in a hybrid with a new phenotype (1); Co-dominance results in a phenotype that is a combination of the two original phenotypes, not a new one (3).

q.q: Unlike complete dominance, where a single dominant allele (e.g. Tt) is enough for full expression of the dominant trait, incomplete dominance requires:
o: No dominant allele at all for expression
Only a single recessive allele for full expression
Two copies of the dominant allele (e.g. RR) for full expression of the trait
Three or more alleles of the same gene
q.e: In incomplete dominance, a single dominant allele (as in Rr) is not enough to produce the full dominant phenotype (red); two copies of the dominant allele (RR) are needed for full expression, unlike complete dominance where one copy (Tt) suffices.

q.q: A red-flowered Mirabilis jalapa plant (RR) is crossed with a pink-flowered plant (Rr). What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
q.e: RR produces only R gametes, and Rr produces R and r gametes in equal proportion, so the cross RR x Rr gives offspring in a 1 RR (red) : 1 Rr (pink) ratio -- no white offspring are possible since no 'r' gamete comes from the RR parent.

q.q: A man with blood group AB (genotype I^A I^B) marries a woman with blood group O (genotype ii). Which blood group(s) can their children have?
o: Only A and B, but never AB or O
A, B, AB or O, all equally likely
q.e: The AB father can pass on either I^A or I^B, while the O mother can only pass on i. So the children's possible genotypes are I^A i (blood group A) or I^B i (blood group B) -- never AB (which needs I^A and I^B together) or O (which needs i from both parents).

q.q: Which of the following statements about phenylketonuria (PKU) is INCORRECT?
o: PKU was first discovered by Folling in 1934
PKU results from a mutation affecting the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
The gene involved in PKU is located on chromosome 12
PKU is inherited as an X-linked dominant trait
q.e: PKU is inherited as an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder, not an X-linked dominant one. It was first discovered by Folling in 1934, and results from a mutation on chromosome 12 affecting phenylalanine hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine.

q.q: By around 1900, which technological advancement allowed scientists to discover and study chromosomes, paving the way for the chromosomal theory of inheritance?
q.e: By 1900, advancement in microscopy allowed chromosomes to be discovered and studied, which enabled Sutton and Boveri to notice the parallel behaviour of chromosomes and genes.

q.q: According to Sutton and Boveri's proposal, which statement correctly describes the parallel behaviour of genes and chromosomes?
o: Genes and chromosomes both occur in pairs, and segregate during gamete formation so that only one of each pair is transmitted to a gamete
Genes occur singly while chromosomes occur in pairs, but both segregate identically
Chromosomes segregate randomly while genes always segregate in a fixed order
Genes and chromosomes show no relationship in their behaviour during meiosis
q.e: Sutton and Boveri proposed that genes and chromosomes both occur in pairs, and both segregate during gamete formation such that only one member of each pair is transmitted to a gamete -- this parallel behaviour forms the basis of the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

q.q: If two genes located on the same chromosome show a recombination frequency of 25%, what is the genetic map distance between them?
q.e: Since 1% crossing over (recombination frequency) between two linked genes equals 1 map unit (Centi Morgan), a recombination frequency of 25% corresponds to a genetic map distance of 25 map units.

q.q: A recombination frequency of 50% between two genes located on the same chromosome would indicate that the genes:
o: Are extremely tightly linked and almost never separate
Behave as if they were on different chromosomes, effectively assorting independently
Have physically switched to a different chromosome
Cannot be mapped using recombination frequency at all
q.e: As physical distance between two genes on a chromosome increases, recombination frequency also increases; at 50% recombination, the genes show no detectable linkage and behave as if they assort independently, just like genes on different chromosomes.

q.q: The chromosomal theory of inheritance is best described as:
o: A theory that replaces Mendelian genetics entirely with chromosome-based rules
The union of the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles
A theory proposed solely to explain sex determination
A theory that applies only to organisms with linked genes
q.e: The chromosomal theory of inheritance is the union of the knowledge of chromosomal segregation (observed under the microscope) with Mendelian principles (inferred from breeding experiments) -- together explaining the physical basis of inheritance.

q.q: Which of the following statements about a male honey bee (drone) is correct, according to the haplodiploid sex-determination system?
o: A drone has both a father and a mother, like any diploid organism
A drone has no father but has a grandfather, and can have grandsons but not sons
A drone always produces daughters through mitosis
A drone is diploid, like a queen or worker bee
q.e: Since a drone develops from an unfertilised egg by parthenogenesis, it has no father, but it does have a grandfather (the father of the queen that laid the unfertilised egg); because drones produce sperm by mitosis (not meiosis), a drone can have grandsons, but since it has no sons of its own (only daughters, if any), the described lineage pattern is a well-known feature of the haplodiploid system.

q.q: In the haplodiploid sex-determination system of honey bees, sex is determined based on:
o: The presence or absence of a Y chromosome
The number of sets (sets of chromosomes, i.e. ploidy) an individual receives, not on distinct sex chromosomes
The number of X chromosomes present, as in the XO system
The temperature at which the egg develops
q.e: Unlike XX/XY or ZW systems that rely on distinct sex chromosomes, sex determination in honey bees is based on the number of sets of chromosomes an individual receives -- fertilised (diploid) eggs become females, and unfertilised (haploid) eggs become males.

q.q: Besides birds, the ZW (female heterogametic) type of sex determination is also seen in some:
q.e: The ZW type of sex determination, in which the female is heterogametic (ZW) and the male is homogametic (ZZ), is seen in birds and also in some reptiles and fishes.

q.q: In grasshoppers, which show the XO type of sex determination, an egg fertilised by an X-bearing sperm develops into a:
q.e: In the XO type of sex determination (e.g. grasshopper), eggs fertilised by X-bearing sperm become females (XX), while eggs fertilised by sperm lacking an X chromosome become males (XO), since no Y chromosome exists in this system.

q.q: In a standard pedigree chart, the individuals belonging to the same generation (siblings) are conventionally arranged:
o: In a random order, with no fixed convention
Below their parents, in order of birth from left to right
Above their parents, in order of birth from right to left
In a circular pattern around their parents
q.e: In pedigree analysis, parents are placed above and their children are placed below, arranged in order of birth from left to right.

q.q: Which of the following statements about standard pedigree chart conventions is INCORRECT?
o: A square represents a male, and a circle represents a female
A diagonal line through a symbol indicates that the individual is deceased
A double horizontal line joining a square and a circle represents monozygotic (identical) twins
An arrow pointing to an individual indicates the propositus/proposita, the starting point of the study
q.e: A double horizontal line joining a square and a circle represents mating between relatives (consanguineous mating), NOT monozygotic twins. Monozygotic twins are shown as two symbols joined at a point that itself joins upward to a single line. The other three statements correctly describe standard pedigree conventions.

q.q: Huntington disease (HD), an example of an autosomal DOMINANT Mendelian disorder, is caused by a mutation in a gene located on which human chromosome?
q.e: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant Mendelian disorder caused by a mutation in a gene located on chromosome 4.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of an autosomal DOMINANT trait?
q.e: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal RECESSIVE disorder, not dominant. Widow's peak, tongue rolling and polydactyly are all examples of autosomal dominant traits.

q.q: Alkaptonuria, an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder, is also known by which common name, referring to a characteristic symptom?
q.e: Alkaptonuria, an autosomal recessive disorder, is commonly known as 'black urine disease' because affected individuals' urine turns black or dark on exposure to air.

q.q: Gaucher's disease, an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder, involves a defective gene located on which human chromosome?
q.e: Gaucher's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder involving a defective gene located on chromosome 1.

q.q: Tay-Sachs disease (TSD), also called Infantile amaurotic idiocy, is an autosomal recessive disorder also known by which other name?
q.e: Tay-Sachs disease (TSD) is also known as Infantile amaurotic idiocy or GM2 gangliosidosis, an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder.

q.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked DOMINANT trait. If the MOTHER is affected (heterozygous) and the father is unaffected, what proportion of their sons and daughters is expected to be affected?
o: None of the sons or daughters
About half of both her sons and her daughters
Only her daughters, none of her sons
q.e: For an X-linked dominant trait, if the female (mother) is affected and heterozygous, about half of her sons and half of her daughters are expected to be affected, since she passes the mutant allele to about half her gametes regardless of the child's sex.

q.q: In X-linked RECESSIVE inheritance (e.g. haemophilia), affected individuals across generations in a pedigree are typically related to one another through the:
o: Paternal side of the family only
No consistent side; the relationship is random
q.e: In X-linked recessive inheritance, affected persons are related to one another through the maternal side of the family, since the mutant allele passes from a carrier mother to her sons.

q.q: Red-green colour blindness (Daltonism), an X-linked recessive disorder, occurs in approximately what percentage of human FEMALES, according to the source material?
q.e: Red-green colour blindness occurs in about 8% of males but only about 0.4% of females, because females have two X chromosomes and so need two copies of the recessive allele to be affected.

q.q: If both parents are red-green colour blind (X-linked recessive), what proportion of their daughters is expected to be colour blind?
q.e: If both parents are colour blind, the father contributes an X-linked recessive allele and the mother (homozygous recessive) contributes another, so all daughters will necessarily be homozygous recessive and colour blind.

q.q: The inclusion of an additional (extra) copy of a chromosome in one homologous pair, represented as 2n+1, is called:
q.e: Trisomy (2n+1) is the inclusion of an additional copy of a chromosome in any one pair of homologous chromosomes, as seen in Down's syndrome (trisomy 21).

q.q: For prenatal diagnosis of chromosomal disorders, cells for karyotype analysis are commonly obtained from amniotic fluid using a procedure called:
q.e: For prenatal diagnosis, cells for karyotype analysis are commonly obtained from amniotic fluid cells collected via amniocentesis, while postnatal karyotyping commonly uses blood lymphocytes.

q.q: Karyotyping is performed on dividing cells arrested at which phase of cell division, when chromosomes are maximally condensed and visible?
q.e: Karyotyping uses dividing cells arrested at metaphase, when chromosomes are maximally condensed and clearly visible under the microscope, allowing their number, size and shape to be studied.

q.q: Cri du chat syndrome, caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, occurs at an approximate rate of:
q.e: Cri du chat syndrome is a rare disorder, occurring at the rate of approximately one in 50,000 live births.

q.q: The term for breast development in males (a symptom of Klinefelter's syndrome, alongside overall masculine development), is:
q.e: Gynaecomastia refers to breast development in males; it is a characteristic symptom of Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY), seen alongside sterility and overall masculine development.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical symptom of Turner's syndrome (45, XO)?
o: A shield-shaped thorax with widely spaced nipples
Gynaecomastia (breast development in the affected individual)
Short stature and absence of secondary sexual characters
q.e: Gynaecomastia (breast development) is a symptom of Klinefelter's syndrome in males, NOT of Turner's syndrome. Turner's syndrome (45, XO) instead shows webbed neck, a shield-shaped thorax with widely spaced nipples, short stature and absent secondary sexual characters, among other features.

q.q: Which of the following is a characteristic clinical feature of Down's syndrome, as described in the source material?
o: A furrowed tongue and a partially opened mouth
A webbed neck and widely spaced nipples
A high-pitched, cat-like cry due to abnormal larynx development
q.e: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) is characterised by short stature, a small round head, a furrowed tongue, a partially opened mouth, a palm crease, congenital heart disease, and mental retardation.

q.q: DNA is a polymer of:
q.e: DNA is a polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; RNA is a polymer of ribonucleotides.

q.q: The bond that joins a nitrogenous base to a pentose sugar in a nucleoside is a:
q.e: Base + sugar = nucleoside, joined through an N-glycosidic bond.

q.q: Nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain are linked by:
q.e: The 3'-OH of one sugar links to the 5'-phosphate of the next, forming the 3'-5' phosphodiester backbone.

q.q: DNA was first isolated from the nucleus and named 'Nuclein' by:
q.e: Meischer identified DNA as an acidic substance present in the nucleus and named it Nuclein.

q.q: In a double-stranded DNA sample, if adenine constitutes 20% of the bases, the percentage of cytosine will be:
q.e: A = T = 20%, so A + T = 40%. The remaining 60% is shared by G and C equally, so C = 30%.

q.q: Which of the following is TRUE of the Watson-Crick DNA model?
o: The pitch is 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs per turn
q.e: The chains are antiparallel and right-handed, the bases project inwards, and one turn of 3.4 nm contains 10 base pairs.

q.q: The number of hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine is:
q.e: A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C through three.

q.q: The stability of the DNA double helix is contributed to by hydrogen bonding and by:
q.e: The plane of one base pair stacks over the next, and this base stacking adds to helix stability.

q.q: The central dogma DNA to RNA to Protein was proposed by:
q.e: Francis Crick proposed the central dogma of molecular biology.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and select the correct option:
q.e: Meischer named Nuclein, Chargaff gave base equivalence, Wilkins and Franklin gave X-ray data, and Temin and Baltimore discovered reverse transcription.

q.q: In a DNA sample, guanine constitutes 30% of the total bases. The percentage of thymine will be:
q.e: G = C = 30%, so G + C = 60%. The remaining 40% is shared equally by A and T, so T = 20%.

q.q: Chargaff's rule of base equivalence (A = T, G = C) strictly applies to:
q.e: Complementary base pairing, on which Chargaff's rule depends, exists only where two strands pair - i.e. double-stranded DNA.

q.q: Purines differ structurally from pyrimidines mainly in having:
q.e: Purines (adenine, guanine) have a double, fused-ring structure, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring.

q.q: If a double-stranded DNA molecule contains 22% thymine, the percentage of guanine in it is:
q.e: T = A = 22%, so A + T = 44%. The remaining 56% is shared equally by G and C, so G = 28%.

q.q: Deoxyadenosine is the nucleoside formed by the union of adenine with:
q.e: Deoxyadenosine = adenine + deoxyribose (via an N-glycosidic bond); adenine + ribose gives adenosine instead.

q.q:
Assertion (A): GC-rich DNA is more thermally stable than AT-rich DNA.
Reason (R): G and C are joined by three hydrogen bonds, while A and T are joined by only two.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
q.e: Both statements are true, and the greater number of hydrogen bonds (three vs two) is exactly why GC-rich DNA requires more heat energy to separate its strands.

q.q: Reverse transcription, the synthesis of DNA from an RNA template, is also known by the name:
q.e: Reverse transcription is also called Teminism, named after Howard Temin, who discovered it along with David Baltimore in 1970.

q.q: A DNA/RNA base sequence is considered incomplete, strictly speaking, unless it is accompanied by its:
q.e: Since every nucleic acid chain has a definite chemical direction, a sequence written without its indicated 5'->3' or 3'->5' polarity is, strictly speaking, incomplete.

q.q: Among the DNA pyrimidine bases, thymine is unique in having:
o: Three hydrogen bonds in every pairing
A ring structure shared with purines
A methyl group not present in cytosine
q.e: Thymine is chemically 5-methyl uracil - it carries a methyl group that cytosine (the other DNA pyrimidine) does not have.

q.q:
How many of the following statements about DNA structure are CORRECT?
1) The sugar-phosphate backbone lies on the outside of the helix
2) The bases project outward, away from the helix axis
3) Nucleotides are joined by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds
4) The two strands run parallel, in the same 5' to 3' direction
q.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong (bases project inward, not outward) and statement 4 is wrong (the strands are antiparallel, not parallel).

q.q:
How many of the following scientist-contribution pairs are CORRECTLY matched?
1) Friedrich Meischer - named the acidic nuclear substance 'Nuclein'
2) Erwin Chargaff - produced the X-ray diffraction data for DNA
3) Watson and Crick - proposed the double helix model in 1953
4) Temin and Baltimore - discovered reverse transcription in 1970
q.e: Pairs 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Pair 2 is wrong - Wilkins and Franklin (not Chargaff) produced the X-ray diffraction data; Chargaff proposed the rule of base equivalence.

q.q:
Assertion (A): A DNA sequence is meaningless unless its 5' to 3' polarity is specified.
Reason (R): Both DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase can synthesise new strands only in the 5' to 3' direction.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
q.e: Both statements are true. Because the polymerising enzymes always read a template and add nucleotides in a fixed 5' to 3' sense, direction is biologically essential, making a sequence without polarity incomplete.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and select the correct option:
q.e: Deoxyribose is the DNA sugar; purines are double-ringed bases; Chargaff's rule states A=T, G=C in equal ratio; base stacking, with H-bonding, stabilises the helix.

q.q: Which of the following pairs INCORRECTLY classifies a nitrogenous base as purine or pyrimidine?
q.e: Cytosine is a pyrimidine (single-ringed), not a purine. Adenine and guanine are the purines; cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines.

q.q:
How many of the following statements about hydrogen bonding and base pairing in DNA are CORRECT?
1) A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds
2) G pairs with C through three hydrogen bonds
3) A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine
4) The diameter of the helix varies depending on which bases are paired at a given point
q.e: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is wrong - because a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, the helix maintains a uniform 20 A diameter throughout, regardless of which specific bases are paired.

q.q: The total length of DNA in a human cell (6.6 x 10^9 bp) is approximately:
q.e: 6.6 x 10^9 bp multiplied by 0.34 x 10^-9 m per bp gives about 2.2 metres.

q.q: The number of base pairs in the E. coli genome is:
q.e: E. coli has 4.6 x 10^6 bp; lambda phage has 48502 bp and the human haploid genome 3.3 x 10^9 bp.

q.q: Histones are basic proteins because they are rich in:
q.e: Lysine and arginine carry positive charges at cellular pH, allowing histones to bind the negatively charged DNA backbone.

q.q: A nucleosome consists of approximately:
o: 200 bp of DNA on a histone octamer
100 bp of DNA on a histone tetramer
400 bp of DNA on a histone hexamer
1000 bp of DNA on NHC proteins
q.e: About 200 bp of DNA winds around a core of eight histone molecules, the histone octamer.

q.q: The 'beads-on-string' structure seen in electron micrographs of chromatin corresponds to:
q.e: Nucleosomes are the repeating units of chromatin, giving the beads-on-string appearance.

q.q: In prokaryotes, DNA is held in large loops in a region called the:
q.e: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; DNA is organised in the nucleoid by positively charged non-histone proteins.

q.q: Which of the following is transcriptionally inactive?
q.e: Heterochromatin is densely packed and darkly stained, making it inaccessible to RNA polymerase and hence inactive.

q.q: Bacteriophage lambda has a genome of:
q.e: Lambda phage contains 48502 base pairs, a standard figure used to show that DNA length is a species characteristic.

q.q: Using 1 nucleotide = 0.34 nm, the length of the single-stranded bacteriophage phi-X174 genome (5386 nucleotides) is approximately:
q.e: 5386 x 0.34 nm = 1831.24 nm, approximately 1.83 micrometres.

q.q: The correct sequence of increasing structural complexity in the packaging of eukaryotic DNA is:
q.e: DNA first winds into nucleosomes (beads-on-string), which further coil into chromatin fibres, which then condense into visible chromosomes at metaphase.

q.q:
Assertion (A): Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA are packaged, but the eukaryotic system is far more elaborate.
Reason (R): Eukaryotic DNA is organised by histones into nucleosomes and further into chromatin fibres, whereas prokaryotic DNA is simply held in loops by non-histone proteins.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
q.e: Both are true, and the multi-level histone-based packaging in eukaryotes versus the simpler loop organisation in prokaryotes is exactly why eukaryotic packaging is described as more elaborate.

q.q: The E. coli genome (4.6 x 10^6 bp) is approximately how many times larger than the bacteriophage lambda genome (48502 bp)?
q.e: 4.6 x 10^6 / 48502 is approximately 95, so the E. coli genome is roughly 95 times larger than lambda's.

q.q: The human haploid genome (3.3 x 10^9 bp) is approximately how many times larger than the E. coli genome (4.6 x 10^6 bp)?
q.e: 3.3 x 10^9 / 4.6 x 10^6 is approximately 717, so the human haploid genome is roughly 700 times larger than that of E. coli.

q.q: Euchromatin and heterochromatin are distinguished under the light microscope mainly on the basis of:
q.e: Euchromatin stains lightly (loosely packed), while heterochromatin stains darkly (densely packed) - a difference visible directly under the light microscope.

q.q: Which of the following is TRUE regarding chromatin organisation?
o: Heterochromatin is loosely packed and lightly stained
NHC proteins form the histone octamer core
Nucleosomes are found only in prokaryotes
Euchromatin corresponds to transcriptionally active regions
q.e: Euchromatin is loosely packed and lightly stained, transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is densely packed, darkly stained and inactive. Nucleosomes are a eukaryotic feature, and NHC proteins are distinct from histones.

q.q:
How many of the following organism-genome size pairs are CORRECTLY matched?
1) Bacteriophage phi-X174 - 5386 nucleotides
2) Bacteriophage lambda - 48502 base pairs
3) Escherichia coli - 4.6 x 10^9 base pairs
4) Human (haploid) - 3.3 x 10^9 base pairs
q.e: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Pair 3 is wrong - E. coli has 4.6 x 10^6 bp, not 4.6 x 10^9 bp.

q.q: Non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins are named so mainly because they:
o: Assist chromatin packaging at higher levels but are not part of the histone octamer
q.e: NHC proteins are an additional set of proteins, distinct from histones, required for packaging chromatin beyond the nucleosome level.

q.q: Using 1 bp/nucleotide = 0.34 nm, the combined length of the bacteriophage lambda genome (48502 bp) and the phi-X174 genome (5386 nucleotides) is closest to:
q.e: 48502 + 5386 = 53888 units; 53888 x 0.34 nm is approximately 18320 nm, i.e. about 18.3 micrometres.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and select the correct option:
q.e: Euchromatin is loosely packed and active; heterochromatin is densely packed and inactive; the nucleoid holds prokaryotic DNA loops; the nucleosome is the eukaryotic packaging unit.

q.q: A defining structural difference relevant to DNA packaging between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell is that a prokaryote lacks a:
q.e: Prokaryotes lack a well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA is scattered in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, unlike the membrane-bound nucleus of eukaryotes.

q.q:
