q.e: Correct count: 2 of 4 statements are correct. Statement 1 is incorrect: GEAC is a government regulatory body that decides the validity of GM research and its public use, not a private seed-selling company. Statement 2 is incorrect: Such modification cannot go beyond proper regulation precisely to avoid loss of biological significance or animal welfare. Statement 3 is correct. Statement 4 is correct.

q.q: In 1983, the American company Eli Lilly successfully produced recombinant human insulin. How many years before the first clinical gene therapy (1990) did this occur?
q.e: 1990 minus 1983 equals 7 years between Eli Lilly's 1983 recombinant insulin and the first clinical gene therapy in 1990.

q.q: Pro-insulin has 3 peptide chains (A, B and C). After the C-peptide is removed, how many chains does mature insulin have?
q.e: Removing the C-peptide from the 3-chain pro-hormone leaves mature insulin with 2 chains, A and B.

q.q: As per the source notes, about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved worldwide, of which 12 are marketed in India. What fraction of the worldwide-approved therapeutics does this represent?
q.e: 12 out of 30 is 12/30 = 2/5, so 2/5 of the worldwide-approved recombinant therapeutics are presently marketed in India.

q.q: If a laboratory has 200 transgenic animals and the source notes state over 95% of all transgenic animals are mice, at least how many of these 200 would be expected to be mice?
q.e: 95% of 200 = 190, so at least about 190 of the 200 transgenic animals would be expected to be mice.

q.q: Rosie's milk contained about 2.4 grams of human alpha-lactalbumin per litre. Approximately how much would be present in 5 litres of her milk?
q.e: 2.4 grams/litre × 5 litres = 12 grams of alpha-lactalbumin in 5 litres of Rosie's milk.

q.q: Bacillus thuringiensis toxins act on three insect orders: lepidopterans, coleopterans and dipterans. How many of these three orders does cry gene technology in Bt cotton specifically target (cotton bollworm, from among these orders)?
o: Only one, since cotton bollworm belongs to a single order (lepidopterans)
q.e: Cotton bollworm is a lepidopteran pest; the cryIAc and cryIIAb genes in Bt cotton specifically target this one order among the three insect orders Bt toxins can act on.

q.q: The Indian Patents Bill received its second amendment to address biopiracy issues, coming after the first amendment. If the first amendment came before the 1997 Basmati patent dispute, the second amendment logically came:
o: After the 1997 dispute, since it was introduced to help deal with such issues
q.e: The second amendment to the Indian Patents Bill was introduced specifically to help deal with biopiracy and patent-related issues such as the 1997 Basmati case, so logically it came after such disputes arose.

q.q: If a pathogen's DNA concentration doubles every PCR amplification cycle starting from 1 copy, how many copies of the target DNA sequence are present after 4 cycles?
q.e: Starting from 1 copy and doubling each cycle: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 after 4 cycles, illustrating why PCR can amplify a target DNA sequence several-fold from a very small starting amount.

q.q: Which of the following statements about Bt cotton is INCORRECT?
o: The cry gene is introduced into the cotton plant genome
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin inside the bacterium
Cotton bollworm is controlled by cryIAb, while corn borer is controlled by cryIAc and cryIIAb
The activated toxin creates pores in midgut epithelial cells
q.e: This reverses the correct pairing: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworm, while cryIAb controls corn borer. The other three statements are correct.

q.q: Which statement about RNA interference is TRUE?
o: Sense and anti-sense RNA anneal because they are complementary
dsRNA is efficiently translated into a silencing protein
RNAi occurs only as a laboratory-invented artificial technique
Agrobacterium is used only to deliver the ADA gene in gene therapy
q.e: Sense and anti-sense RNA, being complementary, anneal to form dsRNA. dsRNA cannot be translated; RNAi occurs naturally as a cellular defence; and Agrobacterium is used in RNAi-based nematode resistance, not in ADA gene therapy.

q.q: Which of the following statements about insulin and gene therapy is INCORRECT?
o: Eli Lilly produced recombinant human insulin in 1983
The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 for ADA deficiency
A retroviral vector introduces ADA cDNA into cultured lymphocytes
A single infusion of engineered lymphocytes gives a permanent cure for ADA deficiency
q.e: Because lymphocytes are not immortal, periodic repeated infusions are needed; a single infusion does not give a permanent cure. The other statements are correct.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes PCR from ELISA?
o: PCR amplifies a target DNA sequence; ELISA is based on antigen-antibody interaction
PCR is based on antigen-antibody interaction; ELISA amplifies DNA
Both PCR and ELISA use autoradiography for detection
Neither PCR nor ELISA can be used for early diagnosis
q.e: PCR amplifies a target DNA sequence several-fold, while ELISA works on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction — two distinct diagnostic principles, both enabling early diagnosis.

q.q: Which of the following statements about transgenic animals is INCORRECT?
o: Transgenic mice are used to test the taste of vaccines before human use
Transgenic animals have manipulated DNA carrying an extra foreign gene
Over 95% of all existing transgenic animals are mice
Alpha-1-antitrypsin, used to treat emphysema, has been produced using transgenic animals
q.e: Transgenic mice are used to test the SAFETY of vaccines (like the polio vaccine) before human use, not their taste. The other statements are correct.

q.q: Which of the following statements about GEAC and biopiracy is TRUE?
o: Biopiracy involves fair compensation always being paid to the resource's country of origin
GEAC decides validity of GM-related research and its use for public utility in India
The 1997 Basmati patent was granted by the Indian Patent Office
Developed nations are generally biodiversity-rich and economically poor
q.e: GEAC's role is correctly stated. Biopiracy specifically lacks fair compensation; the Basmati patent was granted by the US Patent and Trademark Office; and developed nations are economically rich but biodiversity-poor.

q.q: The correct sequence of events in Bt toxin action against a susceptible insect is:
o: Cell lysis → ingestion of crystal → alkaline activation → binding to midgut cells
Ingestion of crystal → alkaline activation → binding to midgut cells → cell lysis and death
Alkaline activation → cell lysis → ingestion of crystal → binding to midgut cells
Binding to midgut cells → ingestion of crystal → cell lysis → alkaline activation
q.e: The insect first ingests the inactive protoxin crystal, the alkaline gut pH activates it, the activated toxin binds midgut epithelial cells, and finally the cells swell and lyse, killing the insect.

q.q: Arrange the steps of RNAi-based nematode resistance in tobacco in the correct order:
o: dsRNA formation → nematode-specific gene introduced → bidirectional transcription → nematode mRNA silenced
Nematode mRNA silenced → dsRNA formation → bidirectional transcription → gene introduced
Bidirectional transcription → gene introduced → nematode mRNA silenced → dsRNA formation
Nematode-specific gene introduced via Agrobacterium → bidirectional transcription → dsRNA formation → nematode mRNA silenced
q.e: The gene is first introduced via Agrobacterium, then transcribed in both directions to give sense and anti-sense RNA, which anneal to form dsRNA, which finally silences the nematode's specific mRNA on infection.

q.q: Arrange the steps of Eli Lilly's 1983 recombinant insulin production in the correct order:
o: Chains joined by disulphide bonds → DNA sequences prepared → introduced into plasmids → chains produced
Chains produced independently → joined by disulphide bonds → DNA sequences prepared → introduced into plasmids
Introduced into plasmids → DNA sequences prepared → joined by disulphide bonds → chains produced
A and B chain DNA sequences prepared → introduced into separate E. coli plasmids → chains produced independently → joined by disulphide bonds
q.e: The A and B chain DNA sequences were first prepared, then introduced into separate E. coli plasmids, the bacteria produced the two chains independently, and finally the chains were joined by disulphide bonds to give mature insulin.

q.q: Arrange the steps of gene therapy for ADA deficiency in the correct order:
o: ADA cDNA introduced → lymphocytes isolated → cultured in vitro → returned to patient
Engineered lymphocytes returned → lymphocytes isolated → cultured in vitro → ADA cDNA introduced
Cultured in vitro → ADA cDNA introduced → returned to patient → lymphocytes isolated
Lymphocytes isolated from blood → cultured in vitro → ADA cDNA introduced via retroviral vector → engineered lymphocytes returned to patient
q.e: Lymphocytes are first isolated from the patient's blood, cultured in vitro, then a functional ADA cDNA is introduced using a retroviral vector, and finally the engineered lymphocytes are returned to the patient's body.

q.q: Arrange the steps of mutation detection by radioactive-probe hybridisation in the correct order:
o: Autoradiography performed → probe prepared → hybridised with DNA → mutated region shows no signal
Mutated region shows no signal → autoradiography performed → probe prepared → hybridised with DNA
Hybridised with DNA → probe prepared → mutated region shows no signal → autoradiography performed
Gene-specific probe prepared → hybridised with patient's DNA → autoradiography performed → mutated region shows no signal
q.e: A gene-specific radioactive probe is prepared first, then hybridised with the patient's DNA, then autoradiography is performed, and a mutated region shows no signal on the resulting film because the probe could not bind there.

q.q: Golden Rice is genetically engineered to be rich in which vitamin?
q.e: Golden Rice is a GM rice variety engineered to be rich in Vitamin A, illustrating enhanced nutritional value.

q.q: Which vector is used to introduce nematode-specific genes into tobacco for RNAi-based resistance?
q.e: Agrobacterium is used as the vector to introduce nematode-specific genes into the tobacco plant.

q.q: About how many recombinant therapeutics have been approved worldwide for human use, as per the source notes?
q.e: About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved worldwide for human use; 12 of these are presently marketed in India.

q.q: A permanent cure for ADA deficiency would require introducing the normal gene into cells at which stage?
o: A very early embryonic developmental stage
q.e: A permanent cure requires introducing the normal ADA gene into cells at a very early embryonic developmental stage, such as bone-marrow stem cells.

q.q: Early diagnosis of a disease by conventional methods is difficult mainly because of which factor?
o: Extremely low pathogen concentration with no visible symptoms yet
The high cost of blood collection
The pathogen being too large to see
q.e: Early diagnosis is difficult because the pathogen concentration is extremely low and symptoms are not yet visible at that stage.

q.q: Rosie, the first transgenic cow, was produced in which year?
q.e: Rosie, the first transgenic cow, was produced in 1997 and produced milk enriched with the human protein alpha-lactalbumin.

q.q: Which body decides on the validity of GM-related research and its use for public utility in India?
q.e: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) decides on the validity of GM-related research and its use for public utility in India.

q.q: Ecology is concerned with which four levels of biological organisation?
o: Cells, tissues, organs and organ systems
q.e: As a branch of biology, ecology studies the relationship of living organisms with the abiotic and biotic components of their environment, at four levels of organisation — organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

q.q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Eurythermal – tolerates only a narrow range of temperature
Stenohaline – tolerates a wide range of salinity
Photoperiodism – bending of a shoot towards light
Salinity – measured in parts per thousand
q.e: Salinity, the salt concentration of water, is measured in parts per thousand (ppt). Eurythermal organisms tolerate a wide temperature range, stenohaline organisms a narrow salinity range, and photoperiodism is the dependence of plants on light for flowering.

q.q: The characteristic features of soil that determine the nature of organisms it can support include:
o: Soil composition, grain size, percolation and water holding capacity
Only the mean annual temperature of the region
Only the salinity expressed in parts per thousand
Only the intensity of light falling on the soil surface
q.e: The nature and composition of soil differ from place to place depending on the climate, the weathering process and the method of soil development; features such as composition, grain size, percolation and water holding capacity decide the organisms it supports.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of escape from stress 'in time' rather than 'in space'?
o: Birds flying from cold regions to warmer regions in winter
A desert lizard moving into the shade at midday
A bacterium forming spores during unfavourable conditions
A seal swimming from one polar sea to another
q.e: Suspension of metabolic activity — spore formation in bacteria and lower plants, hibernation, aestivation and diapause — is escape in time. Migration, on the other hand, is escape in space.

q.q: Thick layer of fat called blubber below the skin of seals in polar seas functions to:
o: Act as an insulator and minimise heat loss
Increase the surface area for heat radiation
Store salts absorbed from sea water
Provide buoyancy for deep diving only
q.e: In the polar seas aquatic mammals like seals have a thick layer of fat (blubber) below their skin that acts as an insulator to minimise heat loss, complementing Allen’s rule and thick fur in other cold-region animals.

q.q: A person newly arrived at Rohtang Pass experiences nausea, fatigue and heart palpitation. The body adjusts to this condition by:
o: Decreasing red blood cell production and slowing breathing
Increasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin only
Lowering the body temperature to conform with the surroundings
Increasing RBC production, decreasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin and increasing breathing rate
q.e: These symptoms are of altitude sickness, caused because the low atmospheric pressure above 3,500 m means the body does not get enough oxygen. Acclimatisation compensates by increased RBC production, decreased haemoglobin binding capacity and an increased breathing rate.

q.q: Birth rate of a human population is expressed as:
o: Total number of children born in a family
Number of live births per one thousand people per year
Ratio of males to females among newborns
Number of individuals inhabiting a particular niche
q.e: Birth rate is the number of live births per one thousand people per year, i.e. per capita births. Death rate is similarly the number of deaths per thousand per year, and both are population attributes, not individual ones.

q.q: A bell shaped age pyramid indicates that the population is:
q.e: The shape of the age pyramid reveals growth status: triangular means an expanding population, bell shaped means a stable population and urn shaped means a declining population.

q.q: Which of the following statements regarding population attributes is INCORRECT?
o: Sex ratio is the ratio of the number of males to females in a population
The structure of the age pyramid determines the growth status of the population
Population density indicates the number of individuals inhabiting a particular niche
An individual organism possesses a birth rate and a death rate of its own
q.e: An individual can be born and can die, but it cannot possess a birth rate or a death rate — these are per capita rates and hence attributes only of a population. The other three statements are correct.

q.q: A rabbit population numbers 100 at the beginning of a year. During that year there are 20 births, 5 deaths, 10 immigrants and 5 emigrants. The population density at the end of the year is:
The integral form of the exponential growth equation is:
q.e: N<sub>t</sub> = N<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup> is the integral form of dN/dt = rN, where N<sub>0</sub> is the density at time 0, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and e = 2.71828. The first option is the logistic equation.

q.q: In a logistic growth curve, the final phase in which the population levels off at the carrying capacity is called the:
q.e: Logistic growth passes through a lag phase, then acceleration and deceleration phases, and finally reaches the asymptote when the population attains the carrying capacity K.

q.q: Competition, as described in this chapter, occurs mainly:
o: Between closely related species sharing the same habitat and food resources
Only between individuals belonging to the same species
Only when the available resources are extremely scarce
Only between a predator and the prey it consumes
q.e: Competition occurs in closely related species which share the same type of habitat and food resources. Resources need not always be scarce, and competition does not necessarily take place between members of the same species only.

q.q: According to the Competitive Exclusion Principle, the competitively inferior species will:
o: Evolve immediately into a new species
Become a predator of the superior species
Always co-exist by raising its birth rate
q.e: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resource cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior species is eliminated eventually.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a defence used by plants against herbivores?
q.e: Plants ward off their predators (herbivores) with thorns, secondary metabolites and poisonous chemicals. Blubber is a thick insulating fat layer in polar aquatic mammals such as seals, and has nothing to do with plant defence.

q.q: Which of the following correctly matches an interaction with its sign notation?
q.e: Amensalism is – / 0 (one species harmed, the other unaffected). Mutualism is + / +, commensalism is + / 0, competition is – / –, and both predation and parasitism are + / –.

q.q: In the fig–wasp mutualism, what does the fig give the wasp in return for pollination?
o: Some of its developing seeds, as food for the wasp larvae
Nectar for the adult female wasp
Protection from the wasp's own predators
Chlorophyll for the wasp to photosynthesise
q.e: The female wasp uses the fig fruit as an oviposition site and pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for egg-laying sites; in return the fig offers some of its developing seeds as food for the developing wasp larvae.

q.q: An orchid growing as an epiphyte on the branch of a mango tree is an example of:
q.e: The orchid gains support and better exposure to light, while the mango tree derives no apparent benefit and suffers no harm. This is a + / 0 interaction, that is commensalism, not parasitism.

q.q: Organisms develop adaptations mainly in order to:
o: Increase the size of their population indefinitely
Survive and reproduce better in their habitat
Avoid interacting with any biotic factor
q.e: Adaptations are characteristics that organisms develop in order to survive and reproduce better in their habitat.

q.q: Large climatic zones on land, produced by seasonal and regional differences in climate, are called:
q.e: Seasonal and regional differences in climate produce large climatic zones on land called biomes, e.g. desert, grassland, tropical forest, temperate forest, coniferous forest and arctic & alpine tundra.

q.q: Biome distribution across the globe is plotted against which two variables?
o: Mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation
q.e: Biome distribution is plotted against two variables: mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation.

q.q: A region with very cold climate throughout the year, regardless of rainfall, is expected to support which biome?
q.e: Very cold regions give rise to the tundra biome, irrespective of precipitation.

q.q: Which of the following is listed as a major biome of India?
q.e: The major biomes of India include tropical rain forest, deciduous forest, desert and sea coast.

q.q: Which of the following is an abiotic factor rather than a biotic factor?
q.e: Abiotic factors are the physico-chemical (non-living) factors such as temperature, water, soil and light; predators, pollinators and competitors are biotic factors.

q.q: Together, the abiotic and biotic factors of a region decide:
o: The rate of mutation in the organism
q.e: Together, abiotic and biotic factors decide which organism can live where, i.e. they define the organism's habitat.

q.q: Temperature is considered the most ecologically relevant abiotic factor mainly because:
o: It has no effect on enzyme activity
All organisms require an optimum temperature for their metabolism and enzyme activity is directly affected by it
It is the only factor that varies with season
It determines the sex ratio of a population
q.e: All organisms require an optimum temperature for their metabolism, and enzyme activity (and hence the whole rate of metabolism) is directly affected by temperature; this is why temperature decides the geographical distribution of most species.

q.q: A fish that can survive only within a narrow temperature range of 24–26°C is best described as:
q.e: Organisms restricted to a narrow range of temperature are called stenothermal (steno = narrow, thermal = temperature).

q.q: An organism capable of tolerating a very wide range of environmental temperatures is called:
q.e: Organisms that can tolerate a wide range of temperature are called eurythermal (eury = wide, thermal = temperature).

q.q: Water is described in this chapter as a major influencing abiotic factor chiefly because:
o: It is always scarce on land
It forms the major constituent of all living cells, and life is impossible without it
It never limits the distribution of organisms
It has no relation to salinity
q.e: Water is a major influencing factor; life on earth is impossible without water because water forms the major constituent of all living cells.

q.q: On land, the limiting factor for organisms is usually the ______ of water, while in the oceans it is usually the ______ of water.
q.e: On land the quantity of water (rainfall) is usually the limiting factor; in the oceans, where quantity is not a limitation, the quality of water (chiefly its salt content) becomes the limitation.

q.q: The salt concentration of water, known as salinity, is expressed in units of:
q.e: The salt concentration of water is measured as salinity, expressed in parts per thousand (ppt).

q.q: An estuarine fish that can tolerate a wide range of salinities, from nearly fresh water to seawater, is described as:
q.e: Organisms that are tolerant of a wide range of salinity, such as many estuarine fishes, are called euryhaline.

q.q: Most freshwater animals cannot survive if placed in sea water, and most marine animals cannot survive in fresh water, mainly because:
o: They lack sufficient light in the new medium
They cannot tolerate the change in soil grain size
q.e: Since most freshwater and marine animals are stenohaline, moving them to water of a very different salinity causes their osmotic balance to collapse.

q.q: The nature and composition of soil at a given place mainly depends on:
o: The climate, the weathering process and the method of soil development
Only the rate of photosynthesis in the area
Only the local sex ratio of animal populations
q.e: The nature and composition of soil differ from one place to another, depending on the climate, the weathering process and the method of soil development.

q.q: Along with pH and mineral content, which soil characteristics determine the vegetation (and hence the animals) of an area?
o: Soil composition, grain size, percolation and water holding capacity
Only the colour of the topsoil
Only the depth of the water table
q.e: Characteristic features such as soil composition, grain size, percolation and water holding capacity, along with pH and mineral content, determine the vegetation of an area, and through the vegetation, the animals that live there.

q.q: In aquatic habitats, the factor corresponding to soil on land, which decides the type of bottom-dwelling (benthic) life, is:
o: The sediment characteristic of the bed
The surface temperature of the water
q.e: In aquatic habitats the corresponding factor to soil is the sediment characteristic of the bed, which decides the type of benthic (bottom-dwelling) life.

q.q: Light is described as the ultimate source of energy for almost every food chain because:
o: It is essential for plants to perform photosynthesis
It directly provides energy to all animals without plants
It controls the salinity of the oceans
It determines the age pyramid of a population
q.e: The Sun is the major source of light; light is essential for plants to perform photosynthesis and hence is the ultimate source of energy for almost every food chain.

q.q: Certain plants of the forest floor, constantly overshadowed by tall trees, become adapted to:
o: Photosynthesise under very low light intensity
Absorb salts instead of light energy
q.e: Certain plants of the forest floor are constantly overshadowed by tall trees and therefore become adapted to photosynthesise under very low light intensity.

q.q: The dependence of flowering in many plants on the duration of light they receive is called:
q.e: Many plants depend on the duration of light for their flowering; this response is called photoperiodism.

q.q: The availability of light for photosynthesis is comparatively higher on land than in water because:
o: Water absorbs and scatters light, limiting photosynthesis in deeper layers
Land receives light only during winter
Water bodies rotate along with the earth's axis
q.e: The availability of light on land is comparatively higher than in water, because water absorbs and scatters light; this limits photosynthesis in deeper layers of oceans and lakes.

q.q: The regular changes in environment that lead to different seasons are primarily brought about by:
o: The rotation of the earth about its axis, along with its revolution and tilt
The migration of birds across continents
q.e: The rotation of the earth about its axis (along with its revolution and tilt) brings about regular changes in the environment, which lead to different seasons.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four levels of biological organisation that ecology is concerned with?
q.e: Ecology is concerned with four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes; cell organelles are not one of these levels.

q.q: Which pair is correctly matched with respect to abiotic factors?
o: Light – essential for photosynthesis and hence the ultimate source of energy for food chains
Soil – has no effect on the vegetation of an area
Salinity – measured only in degrees Celsius
Temperature – has no influence on the geographical distribution of species
q.e: Light is essential for plants to perform photosynthesis, making it the ultimate source of energy for almost every food chain.

q.q: A species is found in scorching deserts as well as in freezing polar regions. This best illustrates that:
o: All species have identical temperature tolerance
Life is found even in harsh and extreme conditions, since organisms get adapted to survive in a wide range of habitats
Such a species cannot be classified under any biome
q.e: Life is found not only in favourable habitats but also in harsh and extreme conditions such as scorching deserts, freezing polar regions and the deep sea, because organisms adapt to survive and reproduce in their habitat.

q.q: Biotic factors of the environment include all of the following EXCEPT:
q.e: Biotic factors are the other living organisms sharing the habitat, such as predators, parasites, competitors, pollinators and symbionts; soil grain size is an abiotic factor.

q.q: Which of the following statements about abiotic factors is CORRECT?
o: Temperature is the most ecologically relevant abiotic factor because it directly affects enzyme activity and metabolism
Salinity is a property of soil rather than water
Light availability is greater in deep ocean water than on land
Stenohaline organisms tolerate a wide range of salinity
q.e: Temperature is the most ecologically relevant abiotic factor because enzyme activity, and hence the whole rate of metabolism, is directly affected by it.

q.q: Match the following combination of climate with the biome it produces: (1) Hot with heavy rainfall (2) Hot with very little rain (3) Very cold regions.
q.e: Hot regions with heavy rainfall give tropical forest; hot regions with very little rain give desert; very cold regions give tundra.

q.q: The maintenance of a constant internal environment by an organism, despite a changing external environment, is called:
q.e: All organisms, in order to sustain maximum functionality, try to maintain a constant internal environment; this maintenance is called homeostasis.

q.q: When conditions become stressful, an organism may adopt one of how many broad strategies?
q.e: When conditions become stressful, an organism may adopt one of four strategies: Regulate, Conform, Migrate or Suspend.

q.q: Animals that maintain a constant body temperature and constant osmolality irrespective of outside conditions are called:
q.e: Regulators are animals with the ability to maintain a constant body temperature and a constant osmolality irrespective of the outside conditions.

q.q: All birds and mammals are examples of:
q.e: All birds and mammals are regulators, able to maintain a constant body temperature (about 37°C in mammals) irrespective of outside temperature.

q.q: Sweating in summer and shivering in winter are examples of physiological responses seen in:
o: Regulators, to keep body temperature constant
q.e: In summer humans sweat (evaporation cools the body) and in winter they shiver (rapid muscle contraction produces heat) — both are regulatory responses that keep body temperature constant.

q.q: Regulation, compared to the other strategies for handling environmental stress, is:
o: Energetically the most expensive strategy, though it gives the greatest independence from the environment
Identical in energy cost to conforming
q.e: Regulation gives the greatest independence from the environment, but it is energetically the most expensive strategy.

q.q: Organisms whose body temperature and osmotic concentration change in accordance with the surrounding medium are called:
q.e: Conformers are organisms whose body temperature changes in accordance with outside temperature; their osmotic concentration also changes with that of the surrounding medium.

q.q: Conformers have generally not evolved into regulators mainly because:
o: Conforming is biologically impossible to change
Regulation is energetically more expensive, and its cost is not worth it for them
All conformers already maintain 37°C body temperature
q.e: Conformers have not evolved into regulators because regulation is energetically more expensive — the cost of thermoregulation and osmoregulation is simply not worth it for them.

q.q: On a graph of internal level versus external level, a regulator is represented by:
q.e: On a graph of internal level versus external level, conformers give a rising straight line, while regulators give a flat horizontal line.

q.q: Organisms that regulate their internal environment only over a limited range of external conditions, and conform beyond that range, are called:
q.e: Partial regulators regulate their internal environment over a limited range of external conditions, and beyond that range they simply conform.

q.q: A bird moving away temporarily from a stressful habitat to a more hospitable region, and returning once the stress period is over, illustrates:
q.e: Migration is escape in space: the organism moves temporarily away from the stressful habitat and returns once the stressful period is over.

q.q: Birds that migrate from cold regions in winter typically:
o: Move to relatively warmer regions, and return again during summer
Never return to their original habitat
Lose the ability to fly permanently
q.e: Birds migrate from cold regions to relatively warmer regions during winter, and back again during summer — a behavioural adaptation to seasonal stress.

q.q: An organism that ceases to be metabolically active during a stressful period and enters a period of dormancy is showing:
o: Escape in time, i.e. suspension of activity
q.e: Some organisms suspend all activity and enter dormancy during a stressful period; this is escape in time.

q.q: Bacteria and lower plants tide over unfavourable conditions mainly by forming:
q.e: Spores are formed in bacteria and lower plants to tide over unfavourable conditions.

q.q: The term for the 'winter sleep' shown by certain animals to escape harsh cold conditions is:
q.e: Hibernation is the winter sleep in animals.

q.q: The term for the 'summer sleep' shown by certain animals to escape harsh heat and dry conditions is:
q.e: Aestivation is the summer sleep in animals.

q.q: Zooplankton entering a stage of suspended development during unfavourable conditions is called:
q.e: Diapause is the stage of suspended development that zooplankton enter during unfavourable conditions.

q.q: Seeds and other vegetative parts of plants tide over unfavourable conditions mainly by:
o: Reducing metabolic activity and entering dormancy, germinating only when conditions are favourable
Developing a thick layer of blubber
q.e: Seeds and other vegetative parts of plants reduce metabolic activity and enter dormancy, germinating only when conditions become favourable.

q.q: Adaptations that describe what an animal actually does, such as basking in the sun or burrowing, are classified as:
q.e: Adaptations may be physiological (internal functioning), behavioural (what the animal does) or morphological (body form and structure); basking and burrowing are behavioural.

q.q: In desert plants, a thick cuticle on the leaf surface and sunken stomata mainly serve to:
o: Check transpiration and reduce water loss
q.e: A thick cuticle checks transpiration, and stomata arranged in deep pits (sunken stomata) reduce water loss.

q.q: The special photosynthetic pathway in many desert plants that allows stomata to remain closed during the day, with CO2 fixed at night, is:
q.e: Desert plants possess CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism), which enables their stomata to remain closed during the day; carbon dioxide is fixed at night instead.

q.q: In Opuntia (a desert cactus), leaves are reduced to spines and photosynthesis is instead carried out by:
q.e: In desert plants like Opuntia, leaves are reduced to spines and photosynthesis is carried out by the flattened green stems.

q.q: Animals of colder regions having shorter limbs and shorter ears, which minimises heat loss, is an example of:
q.e: Shorter limbs and ears in animals of colder regions minimise heat loss; this is Allen's rule, since a smaller surface area relative to volume means less heat is radiated away.

q.q: Places above 3,500 m, such as Rohtang Pass near Manali, present newcomers with altitude sickness mainly because of:
o: Low atmospheric pressure, so the body does not get enough oxygen
Extremely high salinity of the air
q.e: Places above 3,500 m have low atmospheric pressure, so the body does not get enough oxygen; a newcomer suffers from altitude sickness.

q.q: The symptoms of altitude sickness in a newcomer to a high-altitude region typically include:
q.e: A newcomer to high altitude suffers from altitude sickness, with symptoms of nausea, fatigue and heart palpitation.

q.q: The body compensates for low oxygen availability at high altitude by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Decreasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin so oxygen is released more readily
Permanently decreasing red blood cell production
q.e: The body compensates for low oxygen at high altitude by increasing RBC production, decreasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin, and increasing the breathing rate — not by decreasing RBC production.

q.q: The kangaroo rat of North American deserts meets its entire water requirement through:
o: Drinking large amounts of standing water
Absorbing water vapour through its skin
Migrating to wetter habitats every night
q.e: The kangaroo rat meets its entire water requirement through internal oxidation of fat (metabolic water) and has the ability to concentrate its urine, so very little water is lost in excretion.

q.q: A desert lizard basks in the sun when its body temperature drops and moves into the shade as the ambient temperature rises. This is an example of which type of adaptation?
q.e: Basking in the sun and moving into shade in response to temperature is a behavioural adaptation shown by desert lizards.

q.q: Which of the following correctly matches a stress-response strategy with its example?
o: Suspend – a bacterium forming spores during unfavourable conditions
Regulate – a lizard's body temperature changing with the surroundings
Conform – a mammal maintaining 37°C body temperature
Migrate – a plant entering dormancy as a seed
q.e: Suspension of activity, as seen in spore formation by bacteria during unfavourable conditions, is an example of escape in time.

q.q: A population is best defined as:
o: Any single organism living in an area
A group of similar individuals living in a geographical area, sharing similar resources and capable of interbreeding
All the organisms of every species present in a forest
A group of organisms belonging to different species that never interbreed
q.e: A population is a group of similar individuals living in a geographical area, sharing similar resources, and capable of interbreeding.

q.q: Population ecology is considered an important link between ecology and evolution mainly because:
o: Evolutionary changes through natural selection take place at the population level
Only individuals, not populations, undergo natural selection
q.e: Since evolutionary changes through natural selection take place at the population level, population ecology is an important area of ecology that links ecology to evolution.

q.q: Which of the following is a valid example of a population, as used in this chapter?
o: A single teak tree in a forest
All the teak trees of a forest patch
One rat found in an abandoned dwelling
A single lotus plant in a pond
q.e: Examples of populations include all the teak trees of a forest patch, all the rats in an abandoned dwelling, and all the lotus plants in a pond.

q.q: Which of the following is an attribute that a population possesses but an individual organism does not?
q.e: An individual may be born or may die, but only a population has a birth rate and a death rate; individual organisms do not possess this attribute.

q.q: The main attributes unique to a population, as listed in this chapter, include all of the following EXCEPT:
q.e: The main population attributes are birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age distribution and population density; individual body temperature is not a population attribute.

q.q: Death rate (mortality) of a population is expressed as:
o: The total number of deaths recorded in a lifetime
The number of deaths per one thousand people per year, i.e. per capita deaths
The ratio of male to female deaths
The number of individuals inhabiting a niche
q.e: Death rate is the number of deaths per one thousand people per year; it is expressed as per capita deaths.

q.q: Birth rate and death rate of a population are always expressed:
o: As an absolute total number, regardless of population size
Per individual per unit time, so that populations of different sizes can be compared meaningfully
Only once in the entire lifetime of the population
As a percentage of the sex ratio
q.e: Both birth rate and death rate are always expressed per individual per unit time, so that populations of different sizes can be compared meaningfully.

q.q: Sex ratio, as a population attribute, is defined as:
o: The ratio of the number of males to the number of females in a population
The ratio of births to deaths in a population
The ratio of pre-reproductive to reproductive individuals
The ratio of immigrants to emigrants
q.e: Sex ratio is the ratio of the number of males to the number of females in a population.

q.q: The fact that an individual organism cannot have a sex ratio, while a population can, is cited in the chapter as:
o: The clearest proof that sex ratio and similar features are truly population attributes
Evidence that ecology and evolution are unrelated
Proof that populations cannot be measured
q.e: An individual is either male or female and cannot have a sex ratio; only a population can — this is the clearest proof that these are truly population attributes.

q.q: The age distribution plot for a given population is called the:
q.e: The age distribution plot for a given population is called the age pyramid.

q.q: For human populations, the age pyramid is conventionally drawn with which three horizontal bands?
q.e: For human populations the age pyramid is drawn with three horizontal bands — pre-reproductive (bottom), reproductive (middle) and post-reproductive (top) — with males on one side and females on the other.

q.q: An age pyramid that is triangular in shape, with a very broad pre-reproductive base, indicates a population that is:
q.e: An expanding population gives a triangular shaped age pyramid, with a very broad pre-reproductive base.

q.q: An urn-shaped age pyramid, in which the pre-reproductive base is narrower than the reproductive middle, indicates a population that is:
q.e: A declining population gives an urn shaped age pyramid, in which the pre-reproductive base is narrower than the reproductive middle.

q.q: The shape (structure) of the age pyramid of a population is significant mainly because it determines:
o: The exact geographical location of the population
The growth status of the population, i.e. whether it is growing, stable or declining
The carrying capacity of the habitat
q.e: The structure (shape) of the age pyramid determines the growth status of the population — whether it is growing, stable or declining.

q.q: Population size, more technically, is referred to as:
q.e: Population size, more technically, is referred to as population density (N), which indicates the number of individuals inhabiting a particular niche.

q.q: A niche, as used in population ecology, refers to:
o: The exact physical boundary of a habitat
The functional role and position of a species in its habitat
The birth rate of a species
The age pyramid of a species
q.e: A niche is the functional role and position of a species in its habitat — the set of conditions and resources it uses.

q.q: The population density of a huge banyan tree is best expressed, according to this chapter, in terms of:
q.e: Population density need not always be counted as numbers; for a huge banyan tree it may be expressed as biomass.

q.q: The population density of grass or lichens covering an area is most appropriately expressed as:
q.e: Population density, depending on the species, may be expressed as per cent cover, as for grass or lichens.

q.q: When a population is huge and measuring absolute density is time-consuming, ecologists instead measure:
o: Relative density, e.g. the number of fish caught per trap
q.e: If the population is huge, measuring absolute density is time-consuming, so relative density is measured instead — for example, the number of fish caught per trap.

q.q: Counting pug marks or faecal pellets is a method used to estimate the relative density of which animal, as mentioned in this chapter?
q.e: Relative density is measured for tigers, for example, by counting pug marks or faecal pellets, since measuring their absolute density directly is impractical.

q.q: Which of the following statements about a stable population's age pyramid is correct?
o: It is bell shaped, with pre-reproductive and reproductive groups nearly equal
It is triangular, with a very broad pre-reproductive base
It is urn shaped, with a narrow pre-reproductive base
It has no reproductive group at all
q.e: A stable population gives a bell shaped age pyramid; the pre-reproductive and reproductive groups are nearly equal.

q.q: Which of the following pairs of population attribute and its unit of expression is correctly matched?
o: Density of a banyan tree population – biomass
Age pyramid – ratio of males to females alone
q.e: Population density need not always be counted as numbers; for a huge banyan tree it may be expressed as biomass, while grass or lichens may be expressed as per cent cover.

q.q: Match the age pyramid shape with the correct population status: (1) Triangular with broad base (2) Bell shaped (3) Urn shaped.
q.e: A triangular pyramid with a broad base indicates an expanding population, a bell shaped pyramid a stable population, and an urn shaped pyramid a declining population.

q.q: Which of the following statements about birth rate and death rate is CORRECT?
o: Birth rate is expressed as the number of live births per one thousand people per year
Birth rate is a property that an individual organism possesses
Death rate cannot be compared between populations of different sizes
Death rate is always equal to the population density
q.e: Birth rate is the number of live births per one thousand people per year; birth and death rates are expressed per individual per unit time precisely so populations of different sizes can be compared.

q.q: The size of a population is never fixed mainly because it depends on:
o: The availability of food, predation pressure and weather conditions
q.e: Population size is an ever-changing aspect because it depends on the availability of food, predation pressure, weather conditions and similar factors.

q.q: Which of the following factors ADDS to population density?
q.e: Natality (B) is the number of births in a population during a given period and adds (+) to population density.

q.q: Which of the following factors SUBTRACTS from population density?
q.e: Emigration (E) is the number of individuals that have left the habitat during a given period, and it subtracts (–) from population density.

q.q: Immigration, as a factor changing population density, refers to:
o: Individuals of the same species leaving the habitat
Individuals of the same species entering the habitat from elsewhere
The birth of new individuals within the habitat
The death of individuals within the habitat
q.e: Immigration (I) is the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during a given period; it adds to density.

q.q: According to the chapter, which two of the four factors changing population density are normally the most important?
q.e: Normally, natality and mortality are the most important of the four factors; immigration and emigration matter mainly under special conditions.

q.q: In a population, if (B + I) is greater than (D + E) over a given period, the population:
q.e: If (B + I) > (D + E), the population grows; if (B + I) < (D + E), it declines; if they are equal, the population is stable.

q.q: A deer population has, over one year, 40 births, 15 deaths, 8 immigrants and 3 emigrants. Since (B + I) exceeds (D + E), the population over that year:
q.e: Here (B + I) = 48 and (D + E) = 18; since (B + I) > (D + E), the population grows, following N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) – (D + E)].

q.q: A population of 200 individuals experiences 10 births, 10 deaths, 4 immigrants and 4 emigrants in a year. What is the population density at the end of that year?
q.e: Since (B + I) = 14 and (D + E) = 14 are equal, the population is stable and the density remains 200, using N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) – (D + E)].

q.q: A butterfly population of 500 records 60 births, 40 deaths, 5 immigrants and 15 emigrants in a season. The population density at the end of the season is:
Exponential growth of a population occurs when:
o: Resources such as food and space are limited
Resources such as food and space are unlimited, allowing every individual to realise its full reproductive potential
The population has already reached carrying capacity
Immigration and emigration are exactly equal
q.e: Exponential growth occurs when resources (food and space) are unlimited, so every individual can realise its full reproductive potential.

q.q: In the exponential growth equation dN/dt = (b – d) × N, the term (b – d) is replaced by which symbol to give dN/dt = rN?
o: r, the intrinsic rate of natural increase
q.e: Substituting (b – d) = r, where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, gives the standard exponential growth form dN/dt = rN.

q.q: In the equation N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), the symbol 'e' represents:
o: The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The carrying capacity of the habitat
q.e: In N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828).

q.q: A population growing exponentially, when N is plotted against time, gives a curve best described as:
q.e: Plotted against time, exponential growth gives an unbounded J-shaped curve.

q.q: The fact that no species growing exponentially actually covers the whole earth is explained in the chapter by pointing out that:
o: Exponential growth is only a theoretical possibility, since resources in nature are always eventually limited
r is always negative in nature
q.e: Any species growing exponentially would in theory cover the whole earth in a short time, which never actually happens, since resources are not truly unlimited in nature.

q.q: Logistic growth of a population occurs under conditions of:
o: Limited resources, leading to competition between individuals and survival of the fittest
q.e: Logistic growth occurs when resources are limited, which leads to competition between individuals and survival of the fittest.

q.q: The four phases through which logistic population growth passes, in correct sequence, are:
q.e: Logistic growth passes through an initial lag phase, a phase of acceleration, a phase of deceleration, and finally an asymptote at the carrying capacity.

q.q: Carrying capacity (K) of a habitat is defined as:
o: The intrinsic rate of natural increase of a species
The maximum population size the habitat can support with its available resources
The number of births minus the number of deaths
The ratio of males to females in a population
q.e: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population size the habitat can support with its available resources.

q.q: When N is plotted against t for logistic growth, the resulting S-shaped curve is also known as the:
q.e: When N is plotted against t in logistic growth, the result is an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve, called the Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth curve.

q.q: In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN(K – N)/K, when N is very small compared to K, the term (K – N)/K is close to:
q.e: When N is small, (K – N)/K is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential.

q.q: In the logistic growth equation, as N approaches the carrying capacity K, the term (K – N)/K approaches:
q.e: When N approaches K, (K – N)/K approaches 0 and growth stops, i.e. dN/dt = 0.

q.q: The logistic growth model is generally considered more realistic than the exponential model mainly because:
o: No habitat has truly unlimited resources
Exponential growth never occurs at all in nature
Logistic growth always produces a J-shaped curve
Exponential growth requires no birth or death rate
q.e: Because no habitat has truly unlimited resources, the logistic model is considered the more realistic of the two.

q.q: A high intrinsic rate of natural increase (r value), which populations tend to evolve towards to survive better, is referred to in the chapter as:
q.e: Populations tend to increase their reproductive fitness so as to survive better; this is called Darwinian fitness, reflected in a high r value.

q.q: Which of the following species is cited as an example of an organism that breeds only once in its lifetime?
q.e: Pacific salmon fish and bamboo are cited as examples of organisms that breed only once in a lifetime.

q.q: Oysters and pelagic fishes are cited in this chapter as examples of species that produce:
o: A small number of large-sized offspring
A large number of small-sized offspring
No offspring at all, reproducing asexually
Offspring only once in a lifetime, like salmon
q.e: Oysters and pelagic fishes are examples of species that produce a large number of small-sized offspring.

q.q: Birds and mammals, as a life-history strategy, typically produce:
o: A large number of small-sized offspring with no parental care
A small number of large-sized offspring, generally with more parental care
Offspring only once in their lifetime
q.e: Birds and mammals typically produce a small number of large-sized offspring, an evolutionary trade-off associated with greater parental care.

q.q: The evolutionary trade-off between producing many tiny offspring versus few large offspring is best described as:
o: Many tiny offspring mean more parental care and better survival per offspring
Few large offspring mean little parental care and heavy losses
Many tiny offspring mean little parental care and heavy losses, while few large offspring mean more care and better survival per offspring
There is no trade-off; both strategies are always equally successful
q.e: Producing many tiny offspring means little parental care and heavy losses, while producing few large offspring means more care and better survival per offspring.

q.q: Bamboo, which flowers and dies after producing seed only once in its lifetime, is an example of a species that:
o: Breeds many times in a lifetime
Breeds only once in a lifetime
Is a regulator rather than a conformer
q.e: Bamboo, like the Pacific salmon fish, is cited as an example of a species that breeds only once in a lifetime.

q.q: Interactions between two different species of organisms in a habitat are called:
q.e: Interspecific interactions are interactions between two different species of organisms; they may be beneficial or harmful to one or both partners.

q.q: Interspecific interactions are classified according to their outcome for the two partners using which notation?
q.e: Interactions are classified by their outcome for the two partners as + (benefited), – (harmed) or 0 (unaffected).

q.q: Predation is classified with which sign notation, since the predator benefits while the prey is harmed?
q.e: Predation is beneficial to the predator while the prey is harmed — hence it is a + / – interaction.

q.q: Ecologically, predation is important mainly because it acts as a means of:
o: Transfer of energy to the next higher trophic level, and of maintaining balance in the ecosystem
Preventing any species from ever going extinct
Increasing the salinity of aquatic habitats
Causing dormancy in the prey species
q.e: Predation acts as a means of transfer of energy to the next higher trophic level and of maintaining balance in the ecosystem; predators also keep prey populations under control.

q.q: For plants, the organisms that act as predators are considered to be:
o: Herbivores, i.e. grazing and browsing animals
q.e: For plants, herbivores are the predators; grazing and browsing animals are the predators of plants.

q.q: Since plants cannot run away from herbivores, they defend themselves mainly through:
q.e: Because plants cannot run away, they defend themselves morphologically (e.g. thorns) and chemically (e.g. secondary metabolites and poisonous chemicals).

q.q: Thorns on a plant are best described as a:
o: Mechanical (morphological) defence that discourages herbivores from feeding
q.e: Thorns are a mechanical (morphological) defence that discourages herbivores from feeding.

q.q: Secondary metabolites and poisonous chemicals produced by plants mainly serve to:
o: Ward off predators by making the plant distasteful, toxic or indigestible
Increase the plant's rate of photosynthesis
q.e: Secondary metabolites and poisonous chemicals are chemical defences produced to ward off predators, making the plant distasteful, toxic or indigestible.

q.q: Many animals blend with their surroundings to avoid detection by predators; this is called:
q.e: Camouflage — cryptic colouration — allows many animals to blend with their surroundings so that predators do not detect them easily.

q.q: The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predators mainly because:
o: It manufactures a bitter chemical itself using photosynthesis
It acquires a special chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed
It mimics the colour of a venomous snake
It is protected by a thick exoskeleton
q.e: The Monarch butterfly acquires its distasteful chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed; it does not manufacture the chemical itself.

q.q: Competition, as an interspecific interaction, is written with the sign notation:
q.e: Competition is a – / – interaction, because both competing species suffer.

q.q: According to the notes, competition occurs mainly between:
o: Closely related species that share the same type of habitat and food resources
A predator and its prey only
Species that never share the same habitat
Members of a mutualistic pair only
q.e: Competition occurs mainly in closely related species which share the same type of habitat and food resources.

q.q: Which of the following statements about competition, as clarified in this chapter, is CORRECT?
o: Resources need not always be scarce for competition to take place
Competition can only occur between individuals of the same species
Competition never affects the fitness of either species
Competition always leads to immediate extinction of one species
q.e: For competition to take place, resources need not always be scarce, and competition does not necessarily take place only between individuals of the same species.

q.q: In competition between two species, the fitness of one species is significantly lower in the presence of the other, ultimately leading to:
o: Immediate co-evolution into a single species
q.e: In competition, the fitness of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another species, and survival of the fittest ultimately takes place.

q.q: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resource:
o: Can co-exist indefinitely without any change
Cannot co-exist indefinitely; the competitively inferior species is eventually eliminated
Always merge into a single hybrid species
q.e: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resource cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior species will be eliminated eventually.

q.q: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle holds strictly under which condition?
o: When the resource is unlimited and the species barely overlap in requirements
When the resource is limiting and the two species overlap completely in their requirements
Only when one species is a predator of the other
q.e: The Competitive Exclusion Principle holds strictly when the resource is limiting and the two competing species overlap completely in their requirements.

q.q: Some closely related species facilitate their co-existence in nature through resource partitioning, which involves:
o: Altering their feeding time, feeding place or the size of food taken so that overlap is reduced
Migrating permanently to a different continent
q.e: Species may co-exist by resource partitioning, i.e. altering their feeding time, feeding place or the size of food taken, so that the overlap is reduced.

q.q: The fact that many closely related species are actually found living together in the same habitat, despite Gause's principle, is best explained by:
o: Resource partitioning, which reduces the overlap in their requirements
Complete predation of one species by the other
q.e: Some species develop mechanisms such as resource partitioning to facilitate co-existence, which is why many closely related species are found living together in nature.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the ecological role of predators in controlling prey populations?
o: Predators keep prey populations under control, preventing any single prey species from overrunning the habitat
Predators always drive their prey species to complete extinction
Predators have no effect on the size of prey populations
Predators only affect prey populations in aquatic habitats
q.e: Predators keep prey populations under control, so that no single prey species overruns the habitat.

q.q: Which of the following correctly matches a predator defence mechanism with its example?
o: Mechanical defence – thorns discouraging herbivores from feeding
Camouflage – the Monarch butterfly acquiring a toxic chemical from its larval food plant
Chemical defence – cryptic colouration in animals
Resource partitioning – a plant's thick cuticle
q.e: Thorns are a mechanical (morphological) defence; camouflage is cryptic colouration in animals; the Monarch butterfly's toxicity is a chemical defence acquired from its larval food plant.

q.q: Which of the following statements about Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle and resource partitioning is CORRECT?
o: Resource partitioning allows closely related species to reduce the overlap in their requirements and co-exist
Gause's principle states that competing species always merge into one species
Resource partitioning increases the overlap between competing species
The Competitive Exclusion Principle applies only to predator-prey pairs
q.e: Resource partitioning — altering feeding time, place or size of food taken — reduces overlap between closely related species, allowing them to co-exist despite Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle.

q.q: Which of the following statements about competition is INCORRECT?
o: Competition is written with the sign notation – / –
Competition always requires the resource to be extremely scarce
Competition occurs mainly between closely related species sharing the same habitat and food resources
Survival of the fittest ultimately takes place in competition
q.e: For competition to take place, resources need not always be scarce; the other three statements about competition are correct as per this chapter.

q.q: In parasitism, the parasite benefits mainly by:
o: Residing outside or inside the body of the host and getting free accommodation and food
Providing food to the host in exchange for shelter
Being unaffected by the presence of the host
Killing the host immediately upon contact
q.e: In parasitism, the parasite is benefited because it resides outside or inside the body of the host and gets free accommodation and food, while the host is affected due to loss of nutrients.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a special adaptation evolved by parasites?
o: Hooks and suckers for attachment to the host
Loss of the digestive system, absorbing pre-digested food from the host
High reproductive capacity to offset the difficulty of reaching a new host
A thick layer of blubber for insulation
q.e: Parasites have evolved hooks and suckers, loss of the digestive system, and high reproductive capacity; blubber is an adaptation of polar seals, not parasites.

q.q: Parasites that live outside the body of their host are called:
q.e: Ectoparasites live outside the body of the host; examples include lice on humans and ticks on dogs.

q.q: Parasites that live inside the body of their host, such as Plasmodium and tapeworm, are called:
q.e: Endoparasites live inside the body of the host; examples include Plasmodium, liver fluke, tapeworm and roundworm.

q.q: Cuscuta, a parasitic plant commonly found growing on hedge plants, derives its nutrition from the host mainly because it has, in the course of evolution:
o: Developed a thicker cuticle and sunken stomata
Developed a symbiotic relationship with fungi
Evolved a high reproductive capacity only
q.e: Cuscuta has lost its chlorophyll and leaves in the course of evolution and derives its nutrition from the host plant it parasitises.

q.q: Brood parasitism (nest or social parasitism) in birds is best described as:
o: A bird building two nests at once
A parasitic bird laying its eggs in the nest of a host bird, which then raises them
Two bird species sharing a single nest peacefully
A bird migrating to escape predators
q.e: Brood parasitism is seen in birds where the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of an unassuming host bird, which takes care of them until they hatch.

q.q: The classic example of brood parasitism cited in this chapter is:
o: The cattle egret and grazing cattle
The Koel laying its eggs in the nest of the crow
The orchid growing on a mango tree
The clown fish living among sea anemone tentacles
q.e: The classic example of brood parasitism is the Koel laying its eggs in the nest of the crow.

q.q: In commensalism, the outcome for the two partners is best described as:
o: One partner benefited while the other is neither benefited nor harmed
One partner harmed while the other is unaffected
q.e: In commensalism (+ / 0), one partner is benefited while the other is neither benefited nor harmed.

q.q: Barnacles growing on the back of a whale illustrate commensalism mainly because:
o: The barnacles are carried to new feeding grounds while the whale is unaffected
The whale feeds on the barnacles for nutrition
Both barnacles and the whale gain equally from the association
The whale is harmed by the barnacles' weight
q.e: Barnacles growing on the back of a whale are carried to new feeding grounds; the whale is unaffected, making this an example of commensalism.

q.q: Cattle egrets are often seen foraging close to grazing cattle mainly because:
o: The cattle actively hunt insects for the egrets
The cattle, as they move, stir up and flush out insects that the egrets can then catch
The egrets provide grooming services to the cattle
The cattle and egrets compete for the same grass
q.e: Cattle egrets forage close to grazing cattle because the cattle, as they move, stir up and flush out insects from the vegetation that the egrets can then catch.

q.q: In the sea anemone and clown fish association, the clown fish benefits by:
o: Getting protection from predators that stay away from the anemone's stinging tentacles
Feeding directly on the anemone's tentacles
Providing the anemone with nutrients it cannot otherwise obtain
Being harmed by the anemone's sting
q.e: The clown fish lives among the sea anemone's stinging tentacles and gets protection from predators, which stay away from the tentacles; the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit.

q.q: In mutualism, also called symbiosis, the outcome for both partners is:
q.e: In mutualism or symbiosis, both the partners are benefited, written as + / +.

q.q: Lichens represent a mutualistic association between algae and fungi in which:
o: The fungus gives support and shelter to the alga, while the alga prepares food for the fungus
The alga gives support to the fungus while receiving nothing in return
Both partners compete for the same limited resource
The fungus parasitises the alga for nutrients
q.e: In lichens, the fungus gives support (and shelter) to the alga, while the alga prepares the food for the fungus, through photosynthesis.

q.q: Mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants in which:
o: The fungi help the plant absorb essential nutrients from soil, while the plant gives the fungi energy-yielding carbohydrates
The plant absorbs nutrients for the fungi in exchange for shelter
The fungi harm the plant roots while gaining no benefit themselves
The plant provides no benefit to the fungi at all
q.e: In mycorrhizae, the fungi help the plant absorb essential nutrients from the soil, while the plant provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates.

q.q: In the fig–wasp mutualism, the female wasp uses the developing fig fruit mainly to:
o: Feed exclusively on the fig's nectar as an adult
Lay its eggs (oviposition site) and nourish its larvae using the developing seeds
Store metabolic water like a kangaroo rat
q.e: The female wasp uses the fruit as an oviposition site and uses the developing seeds within the fruit to nourish its larvae, while pollinating the fig inflorescence in the process.

q.q: The Ophrys orchid achieves pollination by a species of bee through a strategy known as:
o: Sexual deceit, since a petal resembles the female bee in size, colour and markings
Producing a scent identical to rotting meat
Offering the bee a large nectar reward
Trapping the bee inside a pitcher-shaped leaf
q.e: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs sexual deceit: one petal resembles the female bee, so the male bee 'pseudocopulates' with the flower and is dusted with pollen, which it then transfers to another flower.

q.q: The Ophrys orchid and bee relationship is cited in this chapter as a classic example of:
q.e: The Ophrys orchid and bee relationship, involving sexual deceit for pollination, is a classic example of co-evolution.

q.q: Amensalism is an interaction in which:
o: One species is harmed while the other is unaffected
One species is benefited while the other is unaffected
q.e: In amensalism, one species is harmed while the other is unaffected; the interaction is written as – / 0.

q.q: Amensalism is described as the mirror image of commensalism because:
o: In amensalism both partners are harmed, unlike commensalism
In commensalism one gains and the other is neutral, while in amensalism one loses and the other is neutral
Amensalism always involves predation, unlike commensalism
q.e: Amensalism is the mirror image of commensalism: in commensalism one gains and the other is neutral, while in amensalism one loses and the other is neutral.

q.q: Predation and parasitism share the same + / – sign pattern but are distinguished mainly by the fact that:
o: A predator usually kills and consumes its prey, whereas a parasite generally does not kill the host outright
A parasite always kills its host quickly, unlike a predator
Predation never involves energy transfer, unlike parasitism
Parasitism only occurs in plants, while predation only occurs in animals
q.e: Predation and parasitism are distinguished by the fact that a predator usually kills and consumes its prey, whereas a parasite lives on or in the host and generally does not kill it outright.

q.q: According to the summary table of population interactions, which sign pattern corresponds to mutualism?
q.e: The summary table gives + / + for mutualism, where both partners are benefited.

q.q: Ectoparasitic copepods that infest many marine fish are an example of:
q.e: Ectoparasitic copepods that infest many marine fish are listed as ectoparasites, living outside the body of the host.

q.q: Which of the following correctly matches a population interaction with its example?
o: Mutualism – mycorrhizae between fungi and plant roots
Commensalism – the Koel laying eggs in a crow's nest
Parasitism – barnacles growing on a whale's back
q.e: Mycorrhizae, an association between fungi and plant roots in which both partners benefit, is a classic example of mutualism.

q.q: Which of the following statements about parasitism and predation, taken together, is CORRECT?
o: Both are + / – interactions, but a predator generally kills its prey while a parasite generally does not kill its host outright
Both are + / + interactions in which both partners benefit
A parasite always kills the host immediately, unlike a predator
Parasitism is a – / 0 interaction, unlike predation
q.e: Predation and parasitism share the + / – sign pattern, but a predator usually kills and consumes its prey, whereas a parasite generally does not kill the host outright.

q.q: An ecosystem may be correctly defined as
o: The total number of plant and animal species present in a given area
The interaction of living things among themselves and with their surrounding environment
The vertical distribution of species occupying different levels
The rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
q.e: An ecosystem is the interaction of living things among themselves and with their surrounding environment — a functional unit in which biotic and abiotic components interact.

q.q: Which of the following is the correct example of stratification?
o: Phytoplankton floating on the surface of the ocean in summer
A large tree being fed upon by a very large number of small insects
Accumulation of dark humus in the upper layer of the soil
Trees occupying a higher vertical level than shrubs in a forest
q.e: Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species at different levels; the standard example is that trees occur at a higher level than shrubs.

q.q: The aspects taken into consideration to study the functioning of an ecosystem are
o: Productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling
Productivity, stratification, energy flow and nutrient cycling
Producers, consumers, decomposers and abiotic factors
q.e: The four functional aspects are productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Stratification is structural, the steps of decomposition are a sub-set of one aspect, and the last option lists components, not functions.

q.q: Primary productivity is expressed as
o: Percentage of solar radiation absorbed per year
q.e: Primary productivity, being biomass produced per unit area over a period of time, is expressed either as weight (g m⁻²) or as energy (kcal m⁻²).

q.q: In an ecosystem the gross primary productivity is 100 g m⁻² yr⁻¹ and the respiratory loss is 40 g m⁻² yr⁻¹. The net primary productivity is
q.e: NPP = GPP − R = 100 − 40 = 60 g m⁻² yr⁻¹. This is the biomass available to the consumers of that ecosystem.

q.q: Which of the following statements regarding productivity is INCORRECT?
o: GPP is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers
The annual net productivity of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons of organic matter
NPP is always greater than GPP because respiratory losses are added to it
q.e: NPP = GPP − R, so NPP is always less than GPP; respiratory losses are subtracted, not added. The other three statements are correct.

q.q: The correct sequence of the steps of decomposition is
q.e: Detritus is first fragmented by detritivores, soluble inorganic matter then enters the soil by leaching, catabolism degrades detritus enzymatically, humus accumulates by humification, and finally mineralization releases minerals into the soil.

q.q: Which of the following is resistant to microbial action, decomposes at an extremely slow rate and acts as a reservoir of nutrients?
o: The leachate percolating into the soil
q.e: Humus, formed during humification, is resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly, so it serves as a long-term reservoir of nutrients in the soil.

q.q: Mineralization differs from the other steps of decomposition in that it
o: Is brought about only by earthworms and other detritivores
Converts simple inorganic nutrients into complex organic matter
Occurs only in the complete absence of oxygen
Is an oxygen-consuming process in which humus degrades to release minerals into the soil
q.e: Mineralization is the final step in which humus further degrades to release minerals into the soil. It is an oxygen-consuming process controlled by the chemical composition of the detritus and climatic conditions.

q.q: Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) constitutes what part of the incident solar radiation?
q.e: Plants and other photosynthetic organisms utilise less than 50% of the incident solar radiation, and this usable component is called PAR.

q.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog occupies which trophic level?
q.e: Grass (producer) is the first trophic level, grasshopper (primary consumer) the second, frog (secondary consumer / primary carnivore) the third, and snake the fourth.

q.q: Secondary consumers in an ecosystem are also referred to as:
q.e: Primary consumers are herbivores, secondary consumers are primary carnivores, and tertiary consumers are secondary carnivores.

q.q: Ecological pyramids represent the relationship between different trophic levels in terms of all the following EXCEPT:
q.e: The three ecological pyramids are the pyramid of number, pyramid of biomass and pyramid of energy. Rate of decomposition is not represented by any ecological pyramid.

q.q: In an ideal pyramid of energy, if 1,000,000 J of sunlight is available, the energy present at the level of the secondary consumers is:
q.e: Producers fix 10,000 J (about 1% of sunlight), primary consumers get 1000 J, secondary consumers 100 J and tertiary consumers 10 J.

q.q: Which statement about ecological pyramids is TRUE?
o: Saprophytes occupy the apex of every pyramid
A trophic level represents a functional level and not a single species
The pyramid of energy can be inverted in aquatic ecosystems
A species can belong to only one trophic level at a time
q.e: A trophic level is a functional level; a single species may occupy more than one trophic level at the same time. Saprophytes are given no place in pyramids, and the pyramid of energy is always upright.
